The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1861-d65:
Writing from London on 2 August 1861, Charles Francis Adams laid the post Bull Run picture before Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 65 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

August brought the full weight of the Bull Run defeat to London opinion. Adams reported how ministers and papers now sized up the Union's strength. His letter helped Seward judge how much firmness the British would bear, and how much they would test. Cotton, credit, and pride all pulled London toward the South in that bleak month. Each of those pulls can be felt in the wary tone of his August pages.
frus-1861-d165:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 June 1861. Perry served the American legation in Madrid. The dispatch is document 165 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Legation staff kept the post running between ministers and during absences. Perry's reports from Madrid gave Washington a steady line on Spain. His June letter shows the second tier of the service at work, far from the famous names. Staff men like Perry rarely signed the great notes, yet the record keeps their names. Names of staff men in the headings honor work that great notes often hide.
frus-1861-d265:
A State Department letter of 2 November 1861 told James Shepherd Pike what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 265 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d65:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 15 May 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 65 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d165:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 20 October 1862, and this one is Document 165 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it at the legation in London.

Splitting one day's business into two letters let clerks file each topic apart and let the envoy answer point by point. It also means no single letter holds the whole picture for that date. Read with its same-day pair and the reports Adams sent back, this dispatch helps rebuild a week of Anglo-American dealings in full. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d265:
Dated 8 April 1862, Document 265 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It appears in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward wrote the day after Shiloh's second day ended in Tennessee, though full news had not yet settled. Battles of that scale moved foreign markets and ministries within days. A dispatch sent in their wake carried Washington's framing of events to Paris before French papers fixed their own version, which was half its purpose. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d365:
On 20 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, in a letter printed as Document 365 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward's May letters to Mercier came in the season when France, checked at Puebla, was deciding how deep its Mexican venture would go. Washington's interest was plain: a France busy in Mexico had less freedom to aid the South. The letter is part of the careful spring exchange in which each side measured the other's intentions. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d465:
George Perkins Marsh in Turin received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. It is Document 465 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote four days before Antietam, in the same mid-September round of orders that went to Vienna, Madrid, and The Hague. Marsh's Italy had just been shaken by Garibaldi's clash with royal troops at Aspromonte, news that filled his reports that season. The instruction kept the Turin legation aligned with Washington's line as the war reached its autumn crisis. Small posts received the same careful handling as great ones in Seward's system, and this letter is proof of it.
frus-1862-d565:
Henry Shelton Sanford wrote from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 March 1862. His report is Document 565 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

By March 1862 Union victories in the West had improved the American position in Europe, and Sanford's reports tracked the change from his crossroads post. Belgium's industries felt the war through lost American trade, and its court watched France's Mexican venture with concern. Sanford also kept watch on Confederate agents working in Europe, a duty he pursued with zeal. His spring letter is one of the steady reports by which Washington measured opinion in the smaller capitals that autumn's councils would consult.
frus-1862-d665:
The President of the United States sent this formal letter to the Tycoon of Japan on 1 August 1861. Tycoon was the name American papers used for the shogun, Japan's military ruler. The letter, signed in President Abraham Lincoln's name, is document 665 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Heads of state wrote such letters on great matters of friendship and form, and envoys bore them by hand. This one kept up the bond that Commodore Perry's visit and Townsend Harris's treaty had made in the 1850s. It stands out in the file: amid piles of desk mail, here is the top of both governments speaking at once.
frus-1863p1-d65:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 January 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 65 in part one of the 1863 volume.

The last days of January kept the legation busy with Britain's reading of the war. Adams tracked the press, the public meetings, and the moves of Southern men in London. His reports reached Washington about ten days after he wrote them. This dispatch is one of a same-day pair, part of the near-weekly flow that made the London file the spine of the volume.
frus-1863p1-d165:
Late April brought this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 23 April 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 165 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-April mail from London took stock of a spring that had gone the Union's way on the ships. Adams still watched the yards and the courts, since one held raider did not end the trade. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the legation's watch kept at full care even as the news grew kind.
frus-1863p1-d265:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 August 1863. It is document 265 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d365:
From the British legation in Washington on 19 January 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 365 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Lyons reported each exchange to Lord John Russell in London. What he wrote to Seward, and what Seward answered, shaped British choices about the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d465:
A 16 April 1863 dispatch from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d565:
Document 565 in the volume is a letter of 16 June 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d665:
The 16 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The value of the London file is its view from inside Britain: cabinet moods, press talk, and opinion's turn after Gettysburg and Vicksburg. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0000065:
Yoav Soen, Daniel S. Chen, Daniel L. Kraft, and others reported a new lab method in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their tool uses tiny chip arrays of peptides held by MHC proteins. Those pairs are what T cells scan when they check whether a cell is healthy or infected.

Finding which T cells react to which peptide is slow work with older tools. A chip that tests many pairs at once can spot and sort reactive T cells far faster. That kind of map helps researchers track immune responses during infection or after a vaccine. It can also aid work on immune diseases, where the wrong T cells attack the body's own tissues.
plos-pbio-0020065:
Guang Yao, Mark Craven, Norman Drinkwater, and co-workers used yeast to map a toxic response pathway in PLOS Biology in 2004. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a vertebrate protein that reacts to dioxins and similar pollutants. It switches genes on and off, with effects that include harm to development.

Yeast lacks the receptor, which makes it a clean test bed. The team placed the pathway's parts into yeast and charted the contacts between them, step by step. That kind of map is hard to draw in animal cells, where many signals overlap. Their work lists the players in order and gives toxicology a clearer wiring diagram to test with new compounds.
plos-pbio-0020365:
Mikhail A. Lebedev, Adam Messinger, Jerald D. Kralik, and their team recorded from monkey prefrontal cortex in PLOS Biology in 2004. This front brain area handles planning and working memory. Monkeys did a task where the spot they attended and the spot they had to remember were sometimes different.

Nerve cells in the area coded both kinds of spots, letting the authors compare the two codes side by side. Knowing how attention and memory share or split cell resources is a basic question in brain science. The study gives hard data for models of how the front brain juggles what it sees now with what it must hold for later.
plos-pone-0000065:
Thomas Ruf, Teresa Valencak, Frieda Tataruch, and their team compared mammal running speeds in PLOS ONE in 2006. They found faster mammals tend to have more of a certain fat, called n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, in their muscle membranes. The pattern held across species of very different sizes.

Cell membranes rich in these fats let pumps and signals work faster, which may support quicker muscle action. That would explain why speed tracks membrane makeup so well. The idea links diet and fat chemistry to peak performance in a broad way. It is a neat case of a small chemical trait scaling up to a whole-animal ability that anyone can watch.
plos-pone-0000165:
Juliet R. C. Pulliam, Jonathan G. Dushoff, Simon A. Levin, and colleagues published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines epidemic enhancement in populations where people are only partially immune. Enhancement means a disease can spread or sicken more, not less, when some immunity is already present.

Partial immunity is the norm for many real diseases, from dengue to flu. The authors model when it helps transmission instead of hindering it. Their results warn disease modelers that immunity cannot always be treated as a simple shield, a point with direct bearing on vaccine policy.
plos-pone-0000265:
Piers D. L. Howe and Margaret S. Livingstone published this vision paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Hermann grid illusion is a classic: stare at a grid of black squares and grey spots seem to appear at the crossings. The authors use the cancellation technique, adjusting a real stimulus to null out the illusion, to put a number on its strength.

Measuring an illusion precisely lets researchers test competing explanations of it. The cancellation method turns a subjective effect into a quantity. The paper gives vision science a firmer grip on one of its oldest puzzles, which probes how the retina and brain process contrast.
plos-pone-0000365:
Miguel Viveiros and co-authors examined in PLOS ONE in 2007 how the gut bacterium E. coli responds when antibiotics stress it. Their study links three things. It joins the pressure the drug puts on the cell and the genes the cell switches on in reply. It also tracks changes in how easily things pass through the cell's outer wall.

How permeable a bacterium's wall is can decide whether an antibiotic reaches its target inside. By tying gene responses to wall changes, the study addresses a core problem in drug resistance: bacteria that keep drugs out can survive treatment. The work fits the wider effort to understand how common bacteria adapt to the medicines used against them.
plos-pone-0000465:
Simon Melov and colleagues reported that exercise training rewound gene activity patterns of aging muscle, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As people age, skeletal muscle weakens and its gene expression shifts in characteristic ways. The team tested whether resistance exercise, weight training, could reverse that aging pattern in human skeletal muscle.

The title states their conclusion: resistance exercise reverses aging in human skeletal muscle, at least at the level of gene activity. That molecular evidence complements what trainers observe, that older adults regain strength with training. It also gives researchers measurable markers for testing other interventions meant to slow muscle aging.
plos-pone-0000565:
Nurit Kalderon and colleagues combined two strategies to treat spinal cord injury in an animal model, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury was an acute spinal cord contusion, a bruise like those from car crashes. Their therapeutic strategy paired cell elimination, removing harmful cells, with microsurgical intervention.

Spinal cord injury damages tissue twice: at impact, and again through inflammation and cell death in the hours after. A combined strategy addresses both waves. Studies like this test combinations because single treatments have repeatedly disappointed in this field, where even modest preserved function changes a patient's life.
plos-pone-0000665:
Kimberly A. Kelly, Jonathan Carson, Jason R. McCarthy and co-authors created a peptide tag for imaging inside living bodies, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probes that label specific proteins have become critical for watching biological processes. The team used phage display, a screening method with viruses, to find a short peptide that binds near-infrared fluorochromes very tightly.

They call the peptide the IQ-tag. Near-infrared light passes through tissue better than visible light, so labels glowing in that range suit in vivo imaging. The title says the tag allows protein and cell specific labeling. A small, tight-binding tag can be attached to many targets, widening what doctors and researchers can see.
plos-pone-0000765:
Santanu Mukherjee, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif, Michal Bronstein and colleagues studied how a small virus builds its shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. SV40 is a small DNA virus without an envelope, wrapped in an icosahedral capsid 45 nanometers wide. The outer shell is composed of pentamers, five-unit clusters, of the major capsid protein VP1, linked by flexible arms at their tails.

Assembly builds the shell from those capsomers around the viral minichromosome. The title highlights high cooperativity: VP1 units do not assemble one by one independently, but promote each other's joining. Cooperative assembly explains how hundreds of proteins form one exact shell, a puzzle shared by many viruses.
plos-pone-0000865:
Shawna MacDonald, Gang Song and Chi-Sang Poon asked how breathing syncs with a ventilator, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Keeping a patient's breath in step with the machine is a major concern in intensive care. Lung volume feedback helps set the breathing rhythm, while steady pressure support can push against that rhythm if nothing balances it.

The authors focus on a simple form of learning, one that does not link two events together. They test whether this kind of learning helps the breathing system settle into the machine's pattern. The question matters for anyone designing ventilator care that works with the body rather than against it.
plos-pone-0000965:
Marybeth Langer, Lynn Sniderhan, Ueli Grossniklaus and colleagues described jumping genes leaving from an unusual site, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that move around the genome and reshape it over time. Humans carry no active ones now, but our ancestors did, and their marks remain.

The team focus on excision, the cutting out step, happening at an atypical site. An odd exit point can create a new kind of element in the process. Cases like this show genomes are not fixed texts. They are edited by their own moving parts, sometimes in ways no one predicted.
plos-pone-0001065:
Hiroshi Akashi, Piyush Goel and Anoop John tested how well ancestral sequences can be inferred in fruit flies, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Reading the past state of a gene is critical to spotting the pattern and causes of molecular evolution. Among close relatives, that inference is usually assumed to be robust, but tests of the assumption were limited.

The team examine codon bias evolution in the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup. Codon bias is the uneven use of equivalent DNA spellings for the same building block. If ancestral calls are shaky, conclusions about bias may be too. Their check is methodological ground clearing for a busy field.
plos-pone-0001165:
Before a cell divides, a checkpoint makes sure every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, the machine that pulls chromosomes apart. Théodora Niault, Khaled Hached, and Rocío Sotillo studied a checkpoint protein called Mad2 in female mouse meiosis, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Meiosis is the special division that makes eggs and sperm.

The authors changed Mad2 levels and watched chromosome segregation and checkpoint control in meiosis I. Too much Mad2 is known to hold cells in a prolonged arrest. Their work shows how sensitive egg formation is to the dose of a single checkpoint protein. That matters, because segregation errors cause miscarriage and birth defects.
plos-pone-0001265:
MicroRNAs, tiny regulators of gene activity, were still being discovered species by species in 2007. Thomas Sandmann and Stephen Cohen reported new ones for the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster in a PLOS ONE article that year. The full set of microRNAs was not known for any species, and many were believed to await discovery.

Working from the fly's recently assembled genome, the authors identified novel microRNAs and described how they found them. Each addition to the catalogue sharpens the picture of post-transcriptional regulation in development and disease. The fly, a workhorse of genetics, gains a fuller parts list.
plos-pone-0001365:
Rats communicate with ultrasonic calls that humans cannot hear. Markus Wöhr and Rainer Schwarting asked what one common call type means, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rats emit distinct types of ultrasonic vocalizations depending on age, state, and environment. The 50-kilohertz calls have been proposed as indices of a positive subjective state, a kind of animal contentment.

The authors tested whether playback of 50-kHz calls can induce approach behavior in listening rats. If the calls signal something good, listeners should move toward the sound. Their experiment speaks to how researchers read emotion in laboratory animals, where welfare and data quality both depend on it.
plos-pone-0001465:
Mahamadou Thera and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot tested in Mali. The shot targets a protein on the blood stage of the malaria parasite. The trial enrolled adults who face seasonal malaria in west Africa. It was a phase 1 trial, the first step, focused on safety.

Adults were split at random to get the shot or a control, with the dose raised in steps. The team tracked side effects and immune response in each group. A safe profile with a clear response would earn a trial in children. That is the group malaria hits hardest, so each step toward it counts.
plos-pone-0001565:
Mark Ungrin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on growing human embryo stem cell clumps. Such clumps are the standard way to coax the cells to mature. But hand made clumps vary a lot in size and yield. That spread blurs tests and blocks scale up for care. The team built a way to form clumps in a uniform way.

Their method starts from single cells and yields clumps of set size at high rates. Uniform clumps give cleaner drug and growth tests. They also bring stem cell care closer to a true product. The work fixes a dull but real block in the field.
plos-pone-0001665:
Isabel Leroux-Roels, Roger Bernhard, Pascal Gérard, and their co-authors tested a bird flu vaccine in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The vaccine was built against clade 1 H5N1, one family of the bird flu virus. It was mixed with an adjuvant, an added ingredient that boosts immune responses. A vaccine stockpiled before a pandemic must also work against other families of the virus now spreading in birds.

The team checked whether the clade 1 vaccine raised cross-reactive immunity against clade 2 viruses. The full text gives the trial design, the antibody results, and how broad the protection looked. Broad cross-clade cover is a stated requirement for a pre-pandemic vaccine plan, so these results spoke directly to how health agencies should prepare.
plos-pone-0001765:
Anita M. Hennige and co-authors studied a liver protein tied to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Fetuin-A is secreted by the liver and rises in hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome. Those states come with low-grade inflammation and low levels of adiponectin, a protective fat-tissue hormone.

The team hypothesized fetuin-A helps drive both faults, and report that fetuin-A induces cytokine expression while suppressing adiponectin production. The full text gives the cell and tissue experiments. A single liver protein that fans inflammation and cuts a protective hormone is a plausible drug target. It sits in the cluster of disorders around type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0001865:
Bas B. van Rijn, Arie Franx, Eric A. P. Steegers, and their co-authors tested immune receptor genes in dangerous pregnancy disorders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Altered maternal inflammatory responses play a role in preeclampsia and the HELLP syndrome, a severe variant involving hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Both can kill mother and baby.

The team examined whether variants of the innate immune receptors TLR4 and NOD2, plus a pro-inflammatory phenotype, affect susceptibility to early-onset preeclampsia and HELLP. The full text gives the patient groups and the genetic results. Inherited inflammation settings could one day flag high-risk pregnancies early.
plos-pone-0001965:
Leah Owen and co-authors traced how a cancer-driving fusion protein mutes genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, EWS/FLI, is the master driver of Ewing sarcoma, a bone cancer of the young. Gene studies in a sarcoma cell line had shown the fusion switches more genes off than on. That makes it act in large part as a repressor.

The team followed one target, a gene switch called NKX2.2. As the title states, EWS/FLI represses genes through NKX2.2 during the shift to cancer. Naming the middleman gives drug work a new point of attack in a cancer with few options.
plos-pone-0002065:
Joseph Yu and co-authors followed HIV patients who moved clinics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Long-term retention on antiretroviral therapy in Africa's fast-growing programs was said to be sixty percent at two years. Yet many program reports said little about patients who transferred out to another facility, though Malawi's national figures showed transfers are common.

A patient counted as lost at one clinic may be in care at the next. The team asked what happens to those who transfer out. Fair counting matters: if transfers are thriving elsewhere, programs look worse than they are, and tracing efforts go to the wrong people.
plos-pone-0002165:
Albert Salehi, Sandra Meidute Abaraviciene, Javier Jimenez-Feltstrom, and co-authors studied faulty insulin release in diabetic rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In type 2 diabetes, the beta cells of the pancreas fail to answer rising blood sugar as they should, and in time they fail outright. The team suspected that too much nitric oxide made inside the pancreatic islets plays a part in that failure.

They used GK rats, a strain that develops type 2 diabetes on its own. In these animals, high islet nitric oxide went along with abnormal hormone release. A gut hormone, GLP-1, countered the effect, a clue for how GLP-1 based drugs may protect beta cells.
plos-pone-0002265:
Ivo Dinov, Daniel Rubin, William Lorensen, and co-authors presented a framework for organizing the tools of computational biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Progress in the field rests on three legs: new algorithms, systems to manage data resources, and tools that can work together. Without order, valuable resources sit scattered and hard to find.

iTools is a system for classifying, categorizing, and integrating computational biology resources in one registry. It gives researchers a single place to describe and locate tools and data. Shared registries of this kind keep a fast-growing field from drowning in its own output.
plos-pone-0002365:
Songkun Su, Fang Cai, Aung Si, and co-authors showed that Asian honeybees can read the dances of European honeybees, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The waggle dance lets foragers advertise the place of a food source to hive mates. It is famed as the only known form of symbolic communication in an invertebrate. Whether different honeybee species use the same code was an open question.

In mixed colonies, Asiatic honeybees understood the dance language of European honeybees and found the advertised food. The shared code hints that the dance dialects of bee species rest on a common, older system of spatial communication.
plos-pone-0002465:
Preisser and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Evan L. Preisser, Daniel I. Bolnick, among others. Its subject is the Many Faces of Fear: Comparing the Pathways and Impacts of Nonconsumptive Predator Effects on Prey Populations. Most ecological models assume that predator and prey populations interact solely through consumption: predators reduce prey densities by killing and consuming individual prey.

However, predators can also reduce prey densities by forcing prey to adopt costly defensive strategies. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002565:
Xu, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dao-Zhen Xu, Kai Zhao, Li-Min Guo, among others. Its subject is a Randomized Controlled Phase IIb Trial of Antigen-Antibody Immunogenic Complex Therapeutic Vaccine in Chronic Hepatitis B Patients. The safety of the immune complexes composed of yeast-derived hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002665:
In 2008, Albert Nienhaus and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Interferon-Gamma release assay for the diagnosis of latent TB infection – analysis of discordant results, when compared to the tuberculin skin test. The catalog record names Albert Nienhaus first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. With the Interferon-γ release assays (IGRA) a new method for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infections (LTBI) is available. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002765:
In 2008, Chanaz Salmi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about squalamine: an appropriate strategy against the emergence of multidrug resistant Gram-Negative bacteria?. Authorship is credited in the record to Chanaz Salmi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. We reported that squalamine is a membrane-active molecule that targets the membrane integrity as demonstrated by the ATP release and dye entry. A further point appears in the abstract. In this context, its activity may depend on the membrane lipid composition. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002865:
Jinze Xu and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of iron accumulation with age, oxidative stress and functional decline. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jinze Xu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Identification of biological mediators in sarcopenia is pertinent to the development of targeted interventions to alleviate this condition. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002965:
Davendra Sohal, Andrew Yeatts, Kenny Ye and co-authors combined many microarray studies of blood stem cells in 2008. Microarrays measure gene activity across the genome, and vast data had built up across labs. Combining it is hampered by differing platforms and gene labels between studies.

Their meta-analysis found a novel signature, a shared gene pattern, for hematopoietic progenitor cells, the parents of blood cells. It also showed that data from different platforms can be integrated. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper is both a result and a proof that careful pooling of public data pays off.
plos-pone-0003065:
Qing-Bai She, Sarat Chandarlapaty, Qing Ye and co-authors studied breast tumor response to Akt signaling in a 2008 PLOS ONE article that was later retracted. Faulty PI3K/Akt signaling is common in breast cancers, arising from HER2 amplification, PI3K mutation, or PTEN loss. The objective was to test how Akt activation's role depends on which mechanism switched it on.

Readers should note the retraction status in the catalog title before citing any finding. The paper asked whether tumor cells with PI3K mutation or HER2 amplification depend selectively on Akt. Treat its claims as withdrawn unless independently confirmed elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003165: Hemant Kulkarni and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on judging AIDS risk in people infected with HIV-1. The title states its claim: a combined gene pattern, CCL3L1-CCR5 genotype, improves how well AIDS risk can be assessed. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no data on methods or effect sizes.
plos-pone-0003265:
Deb K. Chatterjee, Kalavathy Sitaraman, Cassio Baptista and colleagues describe a protein array made on demand in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They describe a novel, simple and low-cost protein microarray strategy wherein arrays are generated by printing expression-ready plasmid DNAs onto slides. Those slides can be converted into protein arrays on demand, as the printed plasmids serve dual purposes.

Readers learn how storing DNA instead of protein can solve the fragility of protein chips. Proteins decay fast, while printed DNA keeps until needed. A cheaper, storable array could widen proteomics work beyond specialist centres.
plos-pone-0003365:
Mathieu Lihoreau, Cédric Zimmer and Colette Rivault test mutual mate choice in cockroaches in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Theoretical models of sexual selection predict both males and females of many species should benefit by selecting their mating partners. However, empirical evidence testing and validating this prediction is scarce. In particular, inbreeding avoidance is expected to influence choice by both sexes.

The title states when it pays both sexes to avoid inbreeding, under mutual mate choice. Readers get a rare two-sided test, since most mate choice studies examine females alone. Avoiding inbreeding is a benefit clear enough for both sexes to act on.
plos-pone-0007465:
Yuji Yasukochi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 comparing the chromosomes of two moths: the tobacco hornworm and the silkworm. The silkworm genome is well studied, but most other insects lack such resources. A technique using glowing DNA probes, called BAC-FISH, lets researchers map genes directly onto chromosomes. The team used it to align the two species' karyotypes.

The maps revealed extensive conserved synteny. Long stretches of genes sit in the same order in both moths despite their long separation. That conservation is a practical gift to insect science. Knowledge gained in the silkworm can be transferred to relatives with far less work. The study also gives a picture of how slowly moth chromosomes have rearranged over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0007565:
Jon Kuchenreuther and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was hydrogenases, enzymes that work with hydrogen gas where no oxygen is present. The iron-based kind carry a rare metal core at their heart. Building that core takes help from several other enzymes. Working outside living cells, the team searched for small compounds that speed up the enzyme's start-up in a test system.

Three plain compounds did the job: two amino acids, tyrosine and cysteine, plus a common cell chemical known as SAM. Together they boost the start-up of the hydrogenase in the dish. A good recipe for waking the enzyme outside cells is a real help. It lets researchers study clean hydrogen output under set conditions. Such enzymes draw interest from green-fuel work, since they make hydrogen with no waste. Small compounds that switch them on are handy tools.
plos-pone-0007665:
Joseph Abrajano and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the brain's support cells get their identities. REST is a master regulator that silences neuronal genes outside neurons. It works with partners, including CoREST, at many sites in the genome. The team studied how REST and CoREST are deployed during the making of glia, the brain's support cells. Their focus included oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap neurons in myelin.

REST and CoREST are used in different patterns across glial subtypes. That differential deployment promotes subtype specification and the maturation of the oligodendrocyte lineage. Two related silencers, scheduled differently, produce different cell fates. Myelin-making cells matter in diseases where insulation fails. Understanding their maturation program is a step toward repairing it. The study maps a control layer of brain development that works by repression.
plos-pone-0007765:
Liang Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It searches the genome for markers that predict response to two cancer drugs. The drugs are gemcitabine and AraC, both copies of a DNA building block. Patients vary widely in how they respond to chemotherapy.

The team ran a genome-wide association study using cell line data. They linked DNA variants to how strongly the drugs worked. Such markers are called pharmacogenomic biomarkers. If they hold up in patients, doctors could test DNA before choosing a dose. That promises stronger effects with fewer side effects.
plos-pone-0007865:
Rogier Thurlings and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tracks immune cells moving into inflamed joints in rheumatoid arthritis. In this disease, macrophages drive the inflammation of the joint lining. Studies from the 1960s suggested those macrophages are steadily replaced by monocytes from the blood.

The team used monocyte scintigraphy, a scan that follows labeled monocytes in patients. Imaging shows the dynamics of that migration in living people. If fresh monocytes keep refueling the joint, blocking their entry could calm disease. The scan itself may become a way to measure treatment response.
plos-pone-0007965:
Debbie Liao and colleagues showed how a tumor's neighbor cells help it spread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fibroblasts are support cells, and those tied to cancer are often the tumor's most common neighbor. The team used a mouse model of breast cancer known as 4T1.

The support cells did not just sit by. They reshaped the immune scene around the tumor in ways that fed growth and spread to new sites. That makes them a target in their own right. A drug that calms these helpers might slow the cancer. It would not need to aim at the tumor cells at all.
plos-pone-0008065:
Junfeng Ji and colleagues compared the same master factors in normal and cancer stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Both cell kinds can renew themselves and use the same set of pluripotency factors to do it. The puzzle is why one kind builds healthy tissue and the other builds tumors.

Side-by-side tests showed the factors do unlike jobs in the two settings. A factor that guards healthy renewal may drive growth run wild once the cell is transformed. That split gives drug hunters a hope: hit the cancer use of a factor while sparing its healthy use.
plos-pone-0008165:
Maria D'Orsogna and Tom Chou modeled the best route a virus can take through a host cell in PLOS ONE in 2009. To infect, many viruses must cross the crowded cytoplasm and pass into the nucleus. Along the way their cargo is unpacked and rebuilt into a form fit to enter.

The model weighs speed against that rebuilding: rush, and the cargo arrives unready; linger, and it may be destroyed. An optimal pace sits between. The physics sets bounds every invading virus must obey, and it may show where a drug can tip the balance against the virus.
plos-pone-0008265:
Janet E. Foley and colleagues studied a tick-borne bacterium in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Anaplasma phagocytophilum infects humans and other animals through tick bites. It must live inside host cells to survive. During infection, hosts gain temporary resistance as immunity targets specific antigens. The bacterium varies those antigens to stay ahead.

The team traced that diversity to pseudogenes, broken gene copies held in reserve. Only selected copies are represented, and they cluster in space. Recombining these copies creates fresh antigen variants. Understanding this trick could help design vaccines against the disease it causes, granulocytic anaplasmosis.
plos-pone-0008365:
Jérôme Grimplet and colleagues built a grapevine data network in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Genomic data for grapevine grew exponentially over the previous five years. The Vitis vinifera genome had been sequenced, and transcript, protein, and metabolite data kept coming. The next critical challenge was to provide tools that integrate these layers. Separate data sets alone cannot show how a vine works.

VitisNet integrates omics data through grapevine molecular networks. Networks connect genes to the traits they jointly produce. Wine and grape breeders can use such maps to target quality traits. The resource supports systems-level grape research.
plos-pone-0008465:
Francisco de Castro and co-authors write on reverse evolution in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Some species lose the power to make food from sunlight. That loss has happened many times in the history of life. In fact, loss has occurred more often than gain. Gains gave rise to large groups of algae and plants. Losses came later, as some lines took up other ways to feed.

The paper asks what forces drive such loss. When a trait no longer pays, mutations that break it may spread. The authors weigh drift, selection, and life in new niches. Their account helps explain why a useful trait can vanish.
plos-pone-0008565:
Enn-Ling Chen and co-authors characterize water behavior in MRI in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Contrast in clinical MRI often rests on tissue water proton relaxation. Different tissues relax at different rates, creating image contrast. Yet many aspects of relaxation in complex media are not well understood. Protein solutions and real tissue are such complex media. Limited tools have hampered study of these effects. The team focus on a measure called T1rho dispersion.

They characterize how T1rho varies in protein solutions and tissue. That variation reveals interactions between water and large molecules. Better understanding could improve MRI contrast for disease detection. The paper advances the physics behind a routine clinical tool.
plos-pone-0008665:
Joseph Andrews and co-authors refine a breast cancer signature in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They had found wide DNA methylation changes in a cell model of cancer spread. Methylation is a mark that can silence genes. Those changes came with shifts in chromosome structure. The team now combine tests across several platforms. They merge marks with gene activity and gene copy number in the same cells.

The combined view sharpens the signature of breast cancer spread. Genes both marked and misexpressed become strong candidates. Such a signature may predict which tumors will spread. It also names targets that drugs might block to stop spread.
plos-pone-0008765:
Silvio Notari, Francisco Moleres, Stephen Hunter, and colleagues examined a rare U.S. case of variant CJD. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variant CJD is the human prion disease linked to tainted beef. Most cases occurred in the United Kingdom. Only a few cases were found in the United States. Where the abnormal prion protein hides in the body matters for safety.

Tests found protease-resistant prion protein across many organs. The spread went beyond the brain and tonsils. Such maps inform blood and tissue safety rules. They also show how a foodborne prion can seed the whole body.
plos-pone-0008865:
Manuela Fumagalli, Maurizio Vergari, Patrizio Pasqualetti, and colleagues asked whether the brain handles hard trade-offs differently in men and women. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Utilitarian choices weigh total gain, even when someone gets hurt. Such choices arise in medicine, war, and daily business. The brain circuits behind them were largely unknown. Gender might shape both the choices and the circuits.

Brain stimulation and scanning probed how utilitarian behavior switches on. Results differed between men and women in telling ways. A brain-level account helps explain everyday moral disagreements. The work feeds the young field of moral neuroscience.
plos-pone-0008965:
Gerald Baldridge and co-authors made tick-borne bacteria glow on command, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rickettsia bacteria live only inside other cells and ride blood-feeding arthropods. Some kinds cause typhus and spotted fevers in people. Working with them is hard because they are tricky to change in the lab.

The team rewired Rickettsia montanensis to make a green glowing protein, GFP. They put the glow gene under the bacterium's own ompB switch. When the switch is on, the bacteria light up and can be followed under a microscope. The glow tag gives researchers a new handle on these hard-to-study germs.
plos-pone-0009065:
Charles Kim and co-authors compared heart-risk protein levels across people in a Mayo Clinic study, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cardiovascular disease strikes men and women at different rates. Risk also varies between ethnic groups beyond the usual explanations. The team measured 47 newer protein markers of heart disease.

The study covered 2,561 adults, men and women of varied backgrounds. Many markers sat at different levels by sex or by ethnicity. Such gaps might explain part of the unequal disease burden. Risk scores built on one group's averages could mislead for another.
plos-pone-0009165:
Susu Zughaier and co-authors reworked a cough remedy's chemistry into inflammation fighters, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Noscapine is a plant compound sold over the counter for coughs. It is non-toxic and binds tubulin, the protein scaffolding inside cells. Its shape resembles colchicine, a tubulin drug used against inflammation.

The team tested noscapine and new brominated forms made in the lab. The new forms curbed the cell scaffolding and fought inflammation strongly. A safe old drug's family may yield brand-new medicines this way. The new forms are candidates for diseases driven by runaway inflammation.
plos-pone-0009265:
Venkatesan Radhika and co-authors published this plant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flowers pay pollinating insects in nectar, and most crops depend on that trade. Yet the body signals that control nectar release were little known. Jasmonates, plant hormones famous for aging and defense effects, were the team's suspects.

They tested how jasmonates affect nectar secretion in flowers. These hormones also steer flower development and opening, so a nectar role would fit. Finding the hormone link explains how a plant times its reward to pollinator visits. The knowledge could matter for crops whose yields hinge on insect pollination.
plos-pone-0009365:
Ali Arbab and co-authors published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. After radiation therapy for a brain tumor, scans often cannot tell returning tumor from radiation damage. Both look alike on CT, MRI, and even PET scans. That uncertainty can stall the next treatment decision.

The team labeled killer T cells with magnetic particles, made outside the body. In rats, the labeled cells were tracked by MRI to the injury site. Tumor-seeking immune cells could, in principle, light up real cancer and spare scar tissue. The study tests that approach for separating glioma from radiation injury.
plos-pone-0011465:
Matthew Peirce and co-authors identified in 2010 a scaffold protein that selectively tunes alarm signaling in macrophages. Macrophages spot germs through Toll-like receptors and answer by releasing cytokine alarms. Many proteins pass that signal along, but scaffold proteins decide its strength and flavor by holding the relay team together. The team characterized one such scaffold, Themis2, also called ICB1.

The scaffold regulated macrophage Toll-like receptor signaling in a selective way, affecting some cytokine outputs more than others. A selective knob is more useful than a master switch, since it might calm harmful inflammation without silencing defense entirely. The finding adds a control point on the immune front line. For diseases of runaway inflammation, selective tuning of this kind is exactly what safer drugs will need.
plos-pone-0011565:
Michael Wilson and co-authors tested in 2010 the paradox of carbon monoxide as a lung treatment. The gas is famous as a silent killer in faulty heaters, yet the body makes tiny amounts of it naturally, and small doses calm inflammation in animal studies. The team gave inhaled carbon monoxide to mice with pulmonary inflammation and measured both benefit and safety in the same experiment.

A therapy that is poison at one dose and medicine at another lives or dies on its margin, so testing efficacy and safety together is the honest design. Their results inform whether the gas can soothe injured lungs without harming the animal that breathes it. Inhaled delivery is attractive because the lung, the target, receives the dose first. The study is a careful step in judging a provocative idea, neither dismissing it for its reputation nor trusting it for its promise.
plos-pone-0011665:
Qiong Xue and co-authors traced how anthrax spores break into lung cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Spreading from the airway surface is a critical early step in inhalational anthrax. Recent evidence showed the Bacillus anthracis germ can pass through the lung lining by entering the epithelial cells directly.

The team found entry depends on actin, the cell's structural protein, and requires two signals, c-Src and PI3K. In effect, the spore tricks the cell into pulling it inside. Mapping each step of that break-in exposes points where a drug might block entry before the germ establishes infection.
plos-pone-0011765:
Kristiina Rajamäki and co-authors linked cholesterol crystals to arterial inflammation, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic inflammation of the artery wall is a key element in atherosclerosis, the disease behind most heart attacks. What triggers and sustains that inflammation had remained elusive, though protein complexes called inflammasomes were known to mature inflammatory signals.

The team showed cholesterol crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in human macrophages. Sharp crystals thus act as alarm triggers, not just debris. That crystal-to-alarm link ties cholesterol handling directly to the inflammation driving heart disease and suggests new treatment angles.
plos-pone-0011865:
Richa Tiwary and colleagues investigated in 2010 how a vitamin E relative kills cancer cells. The compound, called alpha-TEA, had already shown anti-cancer effects in lab and animal studies across several tumor types. The team looked at whether stress inside the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein-folding workshop, helps drive the killing.

They connect that stress to a death pathway running through TRAIL and its receptor DR5, which pushes cancer cells into apoptosis, an orderly self-destruction. Showing that two stress systems cooperate gives a fuller account of how the compound works. Details like these help judge which tumors might respond and what drug partners could strengthen the effect.
plos-pone-0011965:
Simone Mocellin and colleagues presented in 2010 a database built to match cancer patients to targeted treatments. Standard cancer therapy still fails many patients, and drugs aimed at specific molecular faults were in their infancy. The missing piece was organized knowledge: which molecular profile calls for which targeted drug.

Their Targeted Therapy Database model links a patient's tumor profile to current knowledge of cancer biology and available targeted options. A structured model matters because the knowledge changes monthly and no clinician can hold it all. Resources of this kind are the plumbing of personalized medicine, turning gene reports into treatment shortlists.
plos-pone-0012065:
Luciano Drager and co-workers measured in 2010 how much sleep apnea adds to the problems of people who already have metabolic syndrome. Obstructive sleep apnea, in which the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, is tightly linked to parts of the syndrome. Most earlier evidence studied single components, or patients already sent to sleep clinics for complaints.

Studying consecutive patients with metabolic syndrome, the team gauged apnea's impact on metabolic and inflammatory markers. That design shows the added burden in an unselected group, not just in people who felt sleepy. If apnea measurably worsens the syndrome's markers, screening for it becomes part of metabolic care rather than an optional extra.
plos-pone-0012165:
Wanlong Ma, Hagop Kantarjian, Xi Zhang, and co-authors reported a rare gene change in blood cancer patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called JAK2 drives several chronic blood diseases, usually through one famous mutation that speeds cell growth. Their lab had tested more than ten thousand samples for that mutation, and a much rarer change, loss of a whole section of the gene, sometimes appears instead.

The authors set out what this rare deletion means for patients who carry it. Rare variants matter because a patient's exact mutation can shape diagnosis, outlook, and drug choice. Cataloguing them keeps genetic testing honest, so an unusual result is read correctly instead of missed or misread.
plos-pone-0012265:
Faten Bougatef, Suzanne Menashi, Farah Khayati, and co-authors studied a surface protein that worsens melanoma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, EMMPRIN, shows up in melanoma tissue where patients fare poorly, but the route from its presence to a worse cancer needed proof. Working with two melanoma cell lines grown from patients' tumors, the team traced what EMMPRIN switches on.

They show it raises a growth-factor receptor on the cancer cells, through a low-oxygen response protein, and that this makes the cells migrate and multiply more. Each named link is a place a drug might cut in. For melanoma, which resists most treatments once spread, a chain of targets beats a single hope.
plos-pone-0012365:
Jayne Sutherland, Bouke de Jong, David Jeffries and colleagues searched blood signals that separate active tuberculosis from silent infection, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of a West African group. TB germs infect about two billion people, and most carry them quietly for life. Doctors need tests that tell who is truly sick now and needs full treatment.

The team measured three signals — TNF alpha, IL-12, and IL-17 — made by blood cells after TB exposure. Together, the pattern of the three split active disease from latent infection well. A blood test built on such signals could speed up diagnosis in clinics that lack advanced labs, helping patients start care sooner.
plos-pone-0012465:
Marcin Piechota, Michal Korostynski and Ryszard Przewlocki built a database of gene switch elements in mammal genomes, described in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes that switch on together often share control elements — short DNA motifs where regulator proteins land. Gene expression datasets let computers hunt those shared motifs across many co-expressed genes at once.

Their database, cREMaG, stores predicted control elements for the mammalian genome in a searchable form. Any researcher can look up a gene set and find its likely switches. Shared public resources of this kind speed up thousands of studies, since each lab need not redo the same genome-wide hunt.
plos-pone-0012565:
Gal Ribak, John Swallow and David Jones filmed diving ducks feeding along the bottom, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Ducks propel themselves underwater with webbed feet, but to stay down and feed they must fight buoyancy the whole time. Earlier views assumed they simply paddled harder; the team measured the actual hydrodynamics and energy cost of holding position.

The ducks use a drag-based hovering method, paddling in a way that resists rising while staying nearly still. The measurements price that hovering in energy, explaining how much food a duck must find to make bottom feeding pay. The work enriches both animal biomechanics and the physics of paddling propulsion.
plos-pone-0012665:
Lin, Liu, Huang and co-authors found dense acid-sensing channels on a little-studied brain cell type. The cells are NG2 glia, a fourth kind of glial cell in the mammal brain that reacts to many kinds of injury. Their 2010 study worked on the rat hippocampus, a region central to memory.

The channels, called ASIC1a, pass calcium and open when tissue turns acidic, as in stroke. Finding so many on NG2 glia gives these quiet cells a possible role in injury response. That role could matter for how the brain heals after damage.
plos-pone-0012765:
Deans, Peterson and Wong described a protein found only in the inner ear's balance and hearing structures. The ear's otoconial membrane holds tiny mineral crystals that sense gravity and motion. Their 2010 paper names the protein otolin, a multi-part glycoprotein specific to the inner ear in mammals.

They show otolin works with two partner proteins in the matrix that holds those crystals. Faults in this system can bring dizziness and balance loss. Naming its parts is a first step toward explaining inherited balance disorders and age-related falls.  The protein builds a mesh that holds crystals in place.
pmc-2724665:
Uttara, Singh, Zamboni, and co-authors review oxidative stress in diseases that destroy nerve cells. Free radicals arise naturally as cells use oxygen for energy. A built-in antioxidant system normally keeps them in check and prevents damage.

Trouble begins when defences fall out of balance and radicals build up or flood in from outside. The review weighs that process in brain diseases and surveys treatment options that act early or late in the chain. Antioxidant therapy is attractive but tricky, and the authors map where it may help most.  Balancing benefit and risk, the authors caution, differs sharply by disease stage.
pmc-2815665: Kabsch published a short paper in 2010 that presents XDS. XDS is a program for work with X-ray data from crystals. Its name is short for X-ray Detector Software. The record kept for this entry is very thin. It gives little more than the program name, its author, and its year. So the paper is best described at that level. It is a specialist software report from the crystal structure field of its time.
pmc-2864565:
Robinson and Oshlack present a scaling normalisation method for comparing gene activity in RNA sequencing data. RNA-seq counts how often each gene is read in a sample. Samples sequenced to different depths cannot be compared raw, since deeper samples simply yield higher counts.

Their empirical scaling method adjusts for those depth differences and for uneven composition between samples. Proper adjustment is what lets a study claim a gene truly rose or fell, rather than merely being counted more. The method became a routine step in RNA-seq analysis pipelines around the world.
pmc-3163565:
Li and Dewey present RSEM, a method for measuring transcript levels from RNA-Seq data accurately. RNA-Seq was transforming how gene activity is measured when they wrote. A key challenge is handling reads that match several genes or several versions of one gene.

Such shared reads are especially tricky when transcripts are built from scratch without a reference genome. RSEM assigns those reads in a principled, probabilistic way instead of discarding them. Accurate counts are the base for every later claim about gene activity, so RSEM became a standard tool in transcript studies.
pmc-4201665:
Braun and Clarke wrote in 2014 for health and wellbeing researchers about thematic analysis. Thematic analysis is a method for finding patterns of meaning in qualitative data, such as interview transcripts. The brief evidence here is the paper's own framing, posed as a question about what this method can offer.

The paper presents thematic analysis as a flexible tool that health researchers can use well. It works across many research questions and does not demand one fixed theory. For fields that rely on people's accounts of illness and care, that flexibility is a real strength. The paper has helped many new researchers choose and carry out this approach with confidence.
pmc-4380465:
Sudlow, Gallacher, Allen, and their colleagues described UK Biobank in 2015. UK Biobank is a large population study set up as an open access resource for research. It was built to find the causes of the complex diseases of middle and old age.

The study follows a large group of volunteers over time and collects health, lifestyle, and genetic data. By linking genes with non-genetic factors, researchers can untangle why diseases arise. Any approved research team can apply to use the data. That openness has made UK Biobank one of the most used health resources in the world.
pmc-5833365:
Beverley Shea, Barnaby Reeves, George Wells, and colleagues introduced AMSTAR 2 in 2017. Systematic reviews guide clinical and policy choices, so their quality matters a great deal. Reviews can be biased, and many now include studies that were not randomized.

AMSTAR 2 is a checklist for judging how well a review was done. It covers the question, the search, study selection, and how results were combined. Some items are marked critical, because a flaw there can ruin the whole review. Appraisers worldwide use the tool to decide which reviews deserve trust before acting on them.
pmc-6208165:
Claudia Tonelli, Iok Chio, and David Tuveson reviewed gene control by the Nrf2 pathway in 2018. Nrf2 is a protein that turns on a broad set of protective genes. Those genes defend cells against toxic and oxidative stress.

The review explains how Nrf2 is held in check in quiet times and freed when stress hits. It maps the genes switched on downstream and the diseases touched by the pathway. Cancer adds a twist, since tumors can hijack this defense to survive treatment. Understanding that balance is key to drugs that raise or block the pathway safely.
pmc-7920465:
Malik Sallam reviewed in 2021 how willing people around the world were to accept a COVID-19 vaccine. Vaccines only control a pandemic if enough people take them, so acceptance matters as much as how well a vaccine works in trials. Sallam gathered studies of acceptance rates among the general public and among health care workers in many countries.

The review compares those rates across places and groups, and notes the wide gaps between them. It also discusses the concerns most often behind reluctance, including safety worries and distrust. Written as vaccination campaigns were just beginning, the review captured an early global snapshot of a challenge that health officials would face throughout the rollout.
plos-pone-0360165:
Jin Guo and Langtao Xing published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It deals with IPT systems, short for inductive power transfer, which send electricity without wires or plugs. The authors focus on choosing the best settings, or parameters, for such a system.

Their tool is the genetic algorithm, a search method that breeds and tests many candidate designs and keeps the strongest ones. Applying it to IPT design is meant to raise efficiency without endless manual trial and error. Engineers working on wireless charging for vehicles and devices are the natural audience for this kind of tuning method.
plos-pone-0346065:
Erik Håkansson and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a rare heart disease. In transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, abnormal protein stiffens the heart. The authors test whether dapagliflozin, a drug first made for diabetes, can reduce symptoms in this condition.

The design is a series of n-of-1 trials run as a pilot study: each patient serves as their own comparison across treatment periods, and results are pooled. That design suits rare diseases where recruiting large trial groups is hard. Cardiologists treating amyloidosis patients are the readers watching whether this drug class earns a place in care.
plos-pone-0359865:
Stefania D'Angelo, Georgia Ntani, Ira Madan, and David Coggon wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on older workers in Britain. It studies early long-term economic inactivity, leaving the workforce for good before retirement age. The findings come from a long-running study of health and work after age fifty, called Health and Employment After Fifty.

The authors weigh factors tied to health, to work, and to social position together, asking which mix pushes people out of work early. Losing experienced workers harms both household incomes and the wider economy. Policymakers trying to keep people working into their sixties, and occupational health teams, are the readers for this breakdown of causes.
plos-pone-0347365:
David Pujal, Guillem Ylla, Agustina Pascual, Josep Bau, and Maria-Dolors Piulachs wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a cockroach, Blattella germanica. It tracks how piRNA expression rises and falls in the ovaries. piRNAs are small RNA molecules that guard the genome, mainly in reproductive tissue.

Expression dynamics means how these molecules rise and fall as eggs develop. In ovaries, piRNAs silence jumping genes that could damage the next generation. Insect biologists use such basic work to understand reproduction in a species that is also a major household pest, and pest control researchers watch for weak points.
plos-pone-0359065:
Catalina Canizares, Francisco Cardozo, Abiraahmi Shankar, Raymond Balise, and Pamela Morris-Perez wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on adolescent health in the United States. It examines whether how much plain water adolescents drink is linked to suicide attempts. The evidence comes from the Youth Risk Behavior Survey covering 2017 to 2021.

That survey is a national school-based record of teen health behaviors. A link between something as basic as water drinking and suicide attempts would more likely mark wider hardship or health habits than a direct cause. School health researchers read such associations as signals to investigate, and this one joins diet to mental health surveillance.
plos-pone-0359565:
Lulu Li and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a census of the NHX gene family across the genome of Forsythia, the spring-flowering shrub. Within that family, the authors single out two members, FsNHX3 and FsNHX6, as the likeliest candidates for roles in the plant's defenses against drought, salt, and cold.

NHX genes manage sodium and acidity inside plant cells, core jobs during stress. Naming the family members and flagging two candidates gives breeders targets for hardier ornamental plants. Plant molecular biologists working on stress tolerance, in shrubs and crops alike, are the readers for this gene census.
plos-pone-0349465: Martínez-Rodríguez and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in genetics on how cells copy their DNA. A harmful change in ORC, a protein complex that starts DNA copying, would normally kill the cell. The team found that changes in other parts, some tied to RNA polymerase II, can cancel that harm. Such rescues reveal how the copying and gene-reading systems back each other up.
plos-pone-0358765:
Anna Szpakowicz leads a team of eight in a 2026 PLOS ONE study searching blood proteins for signs of carotid plaque. This fatty buildup in the neck arteries is an early warning of cardiovascular disease and raises stroke risk, yet it often grows silently. The researchers asked whether a panel of proteins, read by machine learning, could flag who carries plaque before symptoms appear.

They drew on a Polish population study of close to seven hundred adults and measured hundreds of protein markers in each person. Forty-two proteins linked significantly to plaque, and a fingerprint of twenty-five separated people with and without plaque reasonably well in middle aged adults. Md Shahriar Hossain Apu and three colleagues read the public mood about human metapneumovirus from social media, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The respiratory virus, usually mild but dangerous for the elderly and the immune compromised, drew anxious attention during its 2024 outbreak in China and beyond. The team applied sentiment analysis to YouTube discussion to map reactions running from fear to trust, arguing health agencies should know which they face before writing guidance.

Their classifier, built on the XLNet language model, sorted posts with accuracy above ninety-three percent. An explainability layer showed which words and phrases pushed each judgment, so the output can be audited rather than merely believed. The authors pitch the approach as an early listening post for outbreak communication: catch rising fear or carelessness early, answer misinformation precisely, and pitch preventive advice at the audience that actually exists.
plos-pone-0342965:
Richard Fleet led a team of eight authors who studied rural emergency care in Quebec, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Small-town emergency rooms often run short of staff, gear, and backup, while their patients have few other options nearby. The team set out to map the blocks to fair care and rank what should be fixed first.

Fleet's group mixed counts with interviews and open-ended input to build a full-circle view of the problem. Their ranked list gives health planners a clear order of needs, from staffing to transfers to distant hospitals. For rural regions far beyond Quebec, the study shows how to ask local staff what would help most before money is spent.
plos-pone-0358465:
Xiaolin Li led a team of six authors modeling sand behavior under structures, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Dense sand has a quirk called dilatancy: sheared under load, it can expand. That quirk changes how foundations grip, settle, and slip where soil meets concrete or steel.

Li's team built a model whose behavior depends on the sand's current state, then tested how its settings change the results. Engineers can use such a model to predict how structures settle over time. Towers, bridges, and offshore platforms all rest on soil-structure contacts like these. A model that captures expansion under shear helps avoid both costly overdesign and dangerous underdesign in sandy ground.
plos-pone-0358565:
Thomas Muehlbauer led a team of six authors comparing balance training for soccer players, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Players favor one leg, and that imbalance raises injury risk. The team compared training on one leg alone against a combined program that added jump-based plyometric work.

Muehlbauer's group measured balance in still and moving tasks to see which program evened out the legs best. Coaches need that answer in practical form, since training time is limited in a season. A program that cuts asymmetry can lower injury rates while also helping performance. The study speaks to academy and pro settings alike, wherever one-sided sports build one-sided bodies.
plos-pone-0357965:
Samaneh Dehghan led a team of six authors testing light therapy for myelin repair, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Myelin is the insulation around nerve fibers, and its loss underlies diseases such as multiple sclerosis. The team used a model in which a chemical called LPC strips myelin, then tested flickering visual light at a theta rhythm.

Dehghan's non-invasive entrainment approach aims to nudge the brain toward rebuilding myelin without drugs. The team measured both myelin-related changes and functional outcomes. A drug-free lead that improves outcomes in a model is worth attention, since current options for myelin repair are few. Human use is far off, but the direction is fresh.
plos-pone-0357765:

After rotator cuff repair, attention goes to the repaired tendon, but the shoulder blade's own stamina and movement matter too. The team ran a cross-sectional mediation analysis linking blade endurance and abnormal blade movement, called dyskinesis, to functional outcomes.

Alzahrani's findings tell rehabilitation specialists where to focus: the blade, not only the tendon. Mediation analysis helps show the path by which blade problems drag down overall function. Rehab programs can then add blade training with a clearer rationale. For patients, better-targeted therapy may mean a stronger, less painful shoulder in daily life.
plos-pone-0353165:

The team reported the first boreal sable found in Pleistocene deposits of Arctic Siberia, far north of its modern haunts.

That helps scientists reconstruct Ice Age climates and how species shifted as the world warmed. Museum and survey teams also gain a reason to re-examine Arctic collections for overlooked small mammal remains.
plos-pone-0358265:

plos-pone-0358065:
Neil Vaughan published a 2026 modeling paper in PLOS ONE on the paths traced by artificial worms moving through a three-dimensional grid. Each simulated worm follows simple movement rules set by a genetic code, and its trail can end at the starting point, settle into a repeating loop, or keep wandering. Vaughan wrote custom simulation software with three-dimensional graphics and virtual reality views to explore every possible worm type in this new grid setting.

Out of a few thousand unique worms, more than half ended back at the origin and a large share fell into loops, some repeating only after hundreds of thousands of steps. A handful were still running chaotically after tens of millions of steps, with no known outcome. The study shows how very simple rules can generate surprisingly intricate three-dimensional patterns, and it catalogs the odd cases for other modelers to study.
plos-pone-0357565:
Jennifer Andrews and colleagues published a 2026 exploratory study in PLOS ONE on symptom patterns in hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that can affect many body systems at once. Little is known about its cause, so the team looked for symptom groups that travel together, which might point to shared biology. They compared women with the syndrome against matched controls and hypermobile women without chronic pain, scoring pain, energy, mental health, gut, bleeding, and autonomic complaints.

People with the syndrome scored worse in every symptom area. Clustering sorted participants into low, moderate, and high symptom groups. Nearly all controls landed in the low group, while about three in five patients fell in the high group and the rest in the moderate one. Those groupings were reasonably stable under resampling. Such disability patterns, the authors say, can guide future hunts for mechanisms behind the worst-hit symptom clusters.
plos-pone-0355465:
Samantha M. Jones, Faith A. Pasternak, and Erin A. Heerey published a 2026 experiment in PLOS ONE on how appearance-focused TikTok videos change mood through self-objectification, seeing oneself as a body to be judged. More than three hundred women and feminine-identifying participants first rated their tendency to self-objectify. They then watched twenty short videos across five categories, three appearance-focused and two neutral. After each, they reported their state of mind.

People prone to self-objectification slipped into that state more strongly after thinspiration and body-positive clips alike; after thinspiration their negative mood rose more. The twist came with body-positive content: feeling self-objectified there was linked to better mood, not worse. A tendency to self-objectify did not move positive mood in the other categories. The same habit, they say, can cut both ways depending on the message, complicating simple warnings about appearance media.
plos-pone-0357365:

They respond even when the usual genetic markers say they should not. Tumors lacking two famous repair genes respond well, yet some tumors with working copies respond too. The team compared sensitive and resistant lab-grown tumor cells, mapping which proteins cluster with the drug's target.

Sensitive cells carried more of a mismatch-repair protein in that cluster, and lowering that protein made cells less sensitive to the drug. A partner protein also behaved differently after treatment, and lowering it restored sensitivity. Deng and colleagues propose their protein pair as a clue for widening the group of patients who might benefit.
plos-pone-0355965:
