arxiv-2606-16865: A 'quantum billiard' is a particle bouncing chaotically inside a shaped boundary — quantum chaos in a box. This paper studies morphology-resolved scrambling there: how quantum information spreads, resolved by shape. It is for quantum chaos researchers. Chaos, mapped by shape.
20587-integration-of-the-armed-forces-19:
Integration of the Armed Forces, 1940-1965 is an official United States Army history of how the services ended racial segregation. It covers the years from the first wartime pressure for change to the civil rights era. Orders, boards, and battles over policy fill its chapters.

Its author, Morris J. MacGregor, Jr., took his degree in history at the Catholic University of America. He continued graduate study at Johns Hopkins and at the University of Paris on a Fulbright grant. Before joining the Army's history staff, he had trained for years in archives. His book remains the standard account of the policy fight.
21566-the-good-old-songs-we-used-to-sing:
O. H. Oldroyd gathered Union veterans' songs in The Good Old Songs We Used to Sing, '61 to '65. First published in 1882 and reissued in 1902 at ten cents, the book is dedicated to veterans of the war. A photo of General Grant from life, dated 1864, fronts it.

Sherman's March to the Sea leads the set, with tunes drawn from sheet music at the Library of Congress. Other songs recall Resaca, Kennesaw, and the long march down to the sea. Linda Cantoni transcribed the music from the Civil War Songbook and old prints. Old soldiers could sing their war again from these cheap, plain pages.
arxiv-2601-06865: A 2026 arXiv preprint by HALIMA GIOVANNA AHMAD and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers quantum Circuit-Based adaptation for credit risk analysis. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Noisy and Intermediate-Scale Quantum, or NISQ, processors are sensitive to noise, prone to quantum decoherence. And are not yet capable of continuous quantum error correction for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-08365: Malors Espinosa and Zander Karaganis define a generating function for a class of buildings in group theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with buildings of affine type A1, which are trees. The buildings carry an added filtration structure that enriches the count. The authors prove the generating function recovers the zeta function of certain quadratic orders. That bridge links combinatorics of trees to number theory objects. It may give new ways to compute or interpret zeta values through building counts.
arxiv-2601-06665:
Sinchan Rej, Snigdhadev Ray, and Bimalendu Deb propose a Rydberg atom parity gate in 2026. Quantum computation requires two- or multi-qubit controlled gates, they note. Controlled-NOT and controlled-phase gates are the usual building blocks used.

They propose an alternative pathway using a three-qubit parity gate. The gate lives in a Rydberg atom array, they describe. Its basic principle is control by the parity of control qubits. The target qubit's operation depends on that combined parity value. They discuss constructing the gate based on dark state resonances. Parity gates could simplify some simulation and computation circuits considerably. Quantum hardware readers get a design grounded in Rydberg physics. Dark states protect the gate from some common disturbances there.
arxiv-2601-07465:
Jakob Robnik, Uroš Seljak, and colleagues revisit the hardest planet searches from the Kepler space telescope. Kepler's main goal was finding Earth-like planets in the habitable zone around Sun-like stars. Those planets produce tiny, rare dips in starlight when they cross their stars. At that detection limit, Kepler's own pipeline produced unreliable candidates.

False alarms are the central problem: noise and instrument effects can mimic a planet transit. The authors build a pipeline for detection plus false alarm vetting at this limit. Careful vetting decides which faint signals deserve trust and follow-up. The work matters for squeezing real planets out of archival data and for designing searches with future telescopes.
arxiv-2601-07565:
Jiaqi Qiao and colleagues present EGMF, a framework that reads emotion from several signals at once. Emotion recognition names discrete feelings, while sentiment analysis scores overall positive or negative tone. Both tasks benefit from combining text, audio, and visual cues. A face, a voice, and words together say more than any one alone. Their 2026 preprint unifies the two tasks.

EGMF uses expert-guided multimodal fusion together with large language models. Expert guidance shapes how the different signals are merged. The framework handles both discrete emotion labels and continuous sentiment values in one system. That unity simplifies building tools for customer feedback, media analysis, and human-computer interaction. The paper targets scholars in affective computing.
arxiv-2601-07665:
Andrea Martin and Giuseppe Belgioioso teach an algorithm to solve fixed-point problems faster, without losing its safety net. Fixed-point iterations underlie optimization, control, and machine learning. The Krasnosel'skii-Mann iteration is a standard method for nonexpansive mappings. The authors build a learning to optimize framework around it. Their 2026 preprint deliberately adds small perturbations to the standard steps.

The perturbations are summable, meaning their total size stays bounded. That choice improves average performance on a chosen family of problems while keeping convergence guarantees. Speed without guarantees is risky in control and safety settings. Keeping the proof while gaining speed is the paper's selling point. Optimization scholars who distrust black-box learned solvers should find the approach appealing.
arxiv-2601-07765:
Igor Sterner, Alex Lascarides, and Frank Keller teach a model to spot the events that matter most in a story. Narrative salience marks which events drive a story's progression. Their 2026 preprint presents a contrastive learning framework for modeling it. The key device is narrative twins: stories that share the same plot but differ in surface form. Twins let the model separate plot importance from wording.

Contrastive learning pulls matching stories together and pushes others apart in representation space. With twins, the shared signal is the plot itself. A model that learns salience could summarize stories better and track long narratives. It could also help writers see which scenes carry the story. The paper speaks to scholars in computational narrative and natural language processing. It offers data design as the main innovation.
arxiv-2601-08065:
Samuel I. Akinwande and colleagues verify neural controlled systems by working backward from the goal. Reach-avoid specifications demand that a system reach a target while avoiding danger. Forward reachability analysis dominates verification of neural feedback systems. Backward methods have lagged because they scale poorly. Their 2026 preprint introduces algorithms computing both over- and under-approximations of backward reachable sets. Those sets collect states that can reach the goal safely.

Two-sided approximations bracket the true set from outside and inside. That bracket tells engineers how much trust a verdict deserves. Neural controllers in robots and vehicles need such checks before deployment. Backward reasoning starts from the goal, often a smaller set than the start region. The paper serves formal methods and control scholars. It strengthens a weaker side of the verification toolbox.
arxiv-2601-07065:
Eric Feltham wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on two tools for the Julia language. One tool is called FormulaCompiler.jl, and the other is called Margins.jl, and both run in Julia. They deal with marginal effects, which show how a result shifts when one input shifts a bit. Such effects help readers make sense of a fitted model.

Tools in use now can be slow when the data set is large. That slowness caps the size of work a team can do. The new tools aim to lift that cap. Margins.jl gives a clean two-function API. Its plan is a grid with two rows and two cols. One axis picks the base for the test: the whole group or a single profile. The other axis picks the target: effects or forecasts. The paper shows how the grid keeps each task clear and fast.
arxiv-2601-08265: Sebastian Cocks, Salvador Dreo, and Feras Dayoub wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sets out AIMC-Spec, a test set for a radar task. The task is automatic intrapulse modulation classification, or AIMC, used in electronic support systems. It names the kind of modulation built into a single radar pulse, read from its in-phase and quadrature parts. A lack of shared test sets has held back work, above all for weak signals. AIMC-Spec shifts the noise level to test how tools hold up.
arxiv-2601-08465: V. Gorbounov and A. Kazakov wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on round networks of wires and what their edge reads can tell us. The authors use a broad form of the Temperley trick. That trick maps each round network into a totally non-negative Grassmannian. From that map, they show that the true resistance between edge nodes has the Kalmanson property. They then give a full account of which flat networks meet that trait. Such results can help rebuild a hid network from reads at its edge.
arxiv-2601-08765:
Hoang Ly, Emina Soljanin, and Philip Whiting study codes that let a lost part of data be fixed from a few near parts. Such codes guard files spread over many drives. If one drive fails, staff can fix its part with low cost. Most past work set bounds and built codes, but did not test them under real flaws.

The team tests a simple fix rule based on the most common value near the loss. They study its work under both lost parts and wrong parts. Chance math lets them track how often the rule heals the file and how often it fails. A reader who stores large data sets gets a plain rule with clear odds. It may suit fast, cheap fix jobs.
arxiv-2601-08865:
Christopher Lowrance and John Rogers test a class task to lift deep thought in control work. Their class is in mechatronics, the mix of machines, circuits, and code. Two ways to guide a machine are set side by side. One is the classic PID rule. The next is fuzzy logic, which uses soft rules such as a bit too hot.

Pupils work with both rules on like tasks. The pair then check if the side by side work lifts high thought skills. Those skills are to break a task down, to build a fix, and to judge if it works. A reader who teaches such classes gets a task plan with a clear aim. It uses a real clash of methods to push thought past rote steps.
arxiv-2601-08965:
Luisiana Cundin gives a more plain proof for a known wave rule in math physics. The rule is the Newell-Whitehead-Segel equation. It sets how a wave like pattern grows and spreads in space and time. Past work proved the best fit for it is the null, or zero, form. But the path there used deep nests of sums that are hard to read.

New facts on how a mix sum acts let her cut that path short. The new proof gives forms that are far more plain to check. A reader in wave work gets the same end point with less fog. Plain proofs help peers trust a result and teach it with ease.
arxiv-2601-09065:
Yinuo Xu and David Jurgens survey how to treat split calls by human marks in text work. Marks split oft on soft tasks, such as if a text is rude or which side it backs. Old work treats split as noise and takes the most common call. New work says split is a sign. It can show that a text reads in more than one fair way.

The survey gives one view of split aware methods. It spans how to keep split in train data, and how to model each mark hand. It also covers how to grade a tool that may give more than one call. A reader who marks text gets a map of a shift in the field. The crowd may be right in more than one way.
arxiv-2601-09265:
Bei Huang and six co-authors join physics sims to a fast 3D form that can show crisp breaks. The form is built from Gaussian blobs, soft dots that can paint a scene in real time. Past joins of sims to blobs dealt with soft stuff, such as cloth or gel. Hard stuff that cracks was left out. Blobs have no firm in side, so a crack has no place to start.

Their tool is called GaussianFluent. It gives blobs a sound in side with true shade, and a crack aware sim to split them. A reader in film and sim work gets breaks that look true and run fast, a pair that past tools could not hold.
arxiv-2601-09365:
Biswesh Mohapatra and five co-authors study a basic problem in spoken dialog: how people build shared understanding as they talk. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at common ground, the set of things, events, and links that speakers treat as mutually known. The setting is situated dialog, where talk happens in a shared space and stretches over time.

Keeping that shared record straight is hard for machines. The authors argue that dialog systems must store references in a form they can call back later in a chat. The need grows as embodied agents and social robots join human talk. A clear account of common ground would help such systems stay coherent and avoid losing track of what was already settled.
arxiv-2601-09865:
Jacob Sander, Brian Jalaian, and Venkat R. Dasari squeeze large language models for edge deployment. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines Muon-optimized distillation with quantization. Big models strain the compute, memory, and energy budgets of small devices.

Three problems must be solved together: getting task-specific data, fine-tuning for performance, and compressing the model. Distillation trains a small model to mimic a large one; quantization stores weights in fewer bits. The authors optimize the distillation step with the Muon optimizer. A tighter pipeline brings capable language models to phones, drones, and field gear.
arxiv-2601-09965:
Atharva Dange, Ramon Lopez, Nimish Shah, and Louis Deslauriers test an AI tutor for physics work at home. The tool is named aiPlato. It was used in a large first year physics class. The class was at the University of Texas at Arlington.

aiPlato gives step by step hints as pupils work. Two tools sit at its core. One checks a pupil's work on the spot. One is a chat tutor that guides with prompts. The aim is to help while the hard parts stay with the pupil. The paper is a first look at how the class used it.
arxiv-2601-10065:
Vincent Chen, Berndt Müller, and Xiaojun Yao run a gauge theory on a small grid. Gauge rules rule the strong force. The full math is vast. The team cuts each link down to three states. Those states are the null state and two charge states.

With that cut, the model is as lean as it can be. It is named a qutrit cut. The team writes out the full energy rule for two grid shapes. One is a chain of square cells. One is a honeycomb grid in two dims. They then track the pull of a string in the model, a key sign of force bind.
arxiv-2601-10365:
Yan Liu and co authors teach a humanoid robot to run up stairs. For a human, stairs are a small task. For a biped robot, they ask for speed and balance at once. A slip can mean a fall. Most past work walks the robot up at a slow pace.

The team aim for a run, not a walk. Their robot is named FastStair in the work. It learns a gait that is both fast and firm. Steps must land clean at speed. The work tests the gait on real stairs. A fast stair gait would widen where such robots can work.
arxiv-2601-10565:
Dávid Ferenczi, Jean-Gabriel Young, and Leto Peel infer signed ties in social nets from how oft people meet. A signed tie can be warm, cold, or not there at all. Meet data shows who was near whom. But a cold tie and no tie can both yield few meets. Past tools can not split those two.

The team built a tool that can. It asks if a lack of meets came from no chance to meet, or from a wish to avoid. Work and home facts can bound chance. With those in the math, cold ties can be told from null ties. The work sharpens maps of real social nets.
arxiv-2601-10765:
Zubair Shah and Noaman Khan frame neural network pruning as an evolutionary process. Networks are often trained with far more parameters than they need. Many weights turn redundant as learning proceeds. Most pruning methods cut by decree, using importance scores or penalty terms set from above.

That view treats pruning as a central decision imposed on a trained model. Shah and Khan instead stress selection dynamics inside training itself. Sparsity can emerge as some connections win and others fade. The frame borrows the logic of natural selection for model design. It may lead to leaner networks that grow sparse on their own, without a separate cutting stage.
arxiv-2601-11865:
Truong Nguyen, Phi Van Dat, Ngan Nguyen, and their co-authors move preference lessons between models that split text in unlike ways. Distillation lets a small student learn from a big teacher. It is much used in training, but less for aligning models with human taste.

The cross-tokenizer case is the real world case, since models rarely share a text split. That split clash has blocked fine, direct transfer of taste data. Their method, named CTPD in the work, works past that clash. It could let small models gain taste lessons from any strong teacher.
arxiv-2601-11965:
Wanli Wang, Kaixin Zhang, and Yuda Cheng study the far tails of a biased random walk model. The model is the continuous-time random walk, used for how grains spread. Many tests and sims show it fits such spread well.

They treat two cases: Gaussian jumps and discrete jumps. For each, they compute the place spread at short times. They show that a bias brings out exponential decay in the far tails. Tail forms matter, since rare long moves can rule risk and dose.  Short time tails are the core case in their proofs.
arxiv-2601-12165:
Severin Schraven and Simone Warzel give a new matrix product form for fractional quantum Hall wavefunctions. The set spans the Laughlin state and its kin. Their form rests on a strict version of correlators from a chiral quantum field theory.

The form lets them control the coefficients of the Laughlin function times any monomial symmetric polynomial. The expansion uses a Slater determinant or permanent basis. Firm control aids proofs on these topologic states. It also links Hall physics to field theory in a strict way.  The basis is built for states with any particle count.
arxiv-2601-13165:
Bradley McCoy and Binhai Zhu study a watch tower task on rough ground where heights are not exact. In one form the ground is a bent line that moves in one plane, with set cross spots but loose heights. Each height must lie in a given span. In the next form the ground is a mesh of triangles in space, with set flat spots but loose heights.

The team takes the bright side view. They ask for the best tower spot when the true heights turn out as kind as they can. A watch tower must see all of the ground. Their work fits guard and sensor place tasks where ground data is coarse. It shows how to plan well when some facts are spans, not points.
arxiv-2601-13265:
Pedro H. Pereira and co-authors give a micro level theory of quantum friction. Friction at the quantum scale is the drag that two neutral objects feel as they slide past each other. Their route looks at two atoms, both in their low state, in shared motion.

The drag springs from how the atoms' spread out charge clouds reply to the slide. The team states the force as a sum in powers of the slide speed. That form shows which terms lead and which fade. A micro theory of this drag helps staff who build tiny machines and cold atom rigs. At that scale such faint drag can no longer be brushed aside.
arxiv-2601-13365:
Kevin Slote, Jeremie Fish, and Erik Bollt ship a Python pack for causal net finds by an entropy rule. The rule is called optimal causation entropy. It can pull a true causal web from time data of a live system. It can tell a straight link from a path that runs through a mid node.

Their pack is named CausationEntropy. It runs that rule plus key speed ups and growths of the method. The paper marks the pack at its version one state. For teams who study linked oscillators or other live webs, a sound open pack cuts time. It speeds the path from data to a causal map they can test.
arxiv-2601-13465:
Yimeng Min and Carla P. Gomes show that a graph neural net can turn into a heuristic for hard route tasks just by one train run. A heuristic is a fast rule that gives good, not sworn best, answers. Their test task is the travelling salesman task, to find the short tour of a set of towns.

Their net bakes global form binds in as a built in bias. It then gives a tour in one forward pass. No search, no teach marks, and no step by step picks are used. That a plain train path yields a sound tour tool is a surprise. For opt teams, it hints that form bias may swap for search in more tasks.
arxiv-2601-12465:
Miao Peng and five co authors work on teaching language models to reason over long texts. A method called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has boosted short context reasoning. Its gains fade when the context grows long, though. Long tasks need both exact grounding in the text and strong reasoning across far apart parts.

The team propose a fix they call process advantage shaping. The name points to shaping the rewards given to steps of the reasoning process. Better step level signals may push a model to reason in depth, not just skim. The work targets a clear gap: models that ace short problems but falter on long ones. Closing that gap matters for real tasks like long document review.
arxiv-2601-12765:
Zhi Cai and four co authors tackle object detection across domains without source data. Source free object detection adapts a model to a new domain without revisiting source images. That setting fits privacy and storage limits in real deployments. Existing methods suffer from source bias, though: the adapted model stays skewed toward the source domain.

That skew leads to poor generalization on the target domain. It also causes error accumulation during self training, as bad labels reinforce themselves. The team use vision foundation models toward unbiased adaptation. Their work was prepared for a pattern recognition journal. Reliable source free detection would ease deployment of vision systems in new places.
arxiv-2601-12965:
Doheon Kim studies the sampling dynamics of score based diffusion models under a special conditioning trick. Diffusion models generate samples by learning the score function of a diffusion process. Theory explains their success through differential equations tied to sampling. Earlier work by Song and Ermon showed a puzzle in this story.

Neural networks using multiplicative noise conditioning still generated satisfactory samples. That fact sits oddly with the standard theoretical picture. Kim examines the deterministic dynamics of sampling in that setting. Clarifying why the trick works could improve sampler design. The work serves the theory of generative modeling, a fast moving field.
arxiv-2601-14365:
Tianhong Lu and Luiz H. Santos study paired quantum particles in this 2026 paper. Their materials are transition-metal dichalcogenides, thin crystals known as TMDs. These crystals host topological electronic states with no external magnetic field. They also show a strong optical response from long-lived excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole.

The team joins those two traits. They study an interacting fermion-boson system made by coupling an exciton to a quasihole. The quasihole sits in a fractional Chern insulator at filling fraction one third. Their title points to spectral fingerprints, marks in the spectrum that would show the exciton-anyon binding they study.
arxiv-2601-14465:
Máté Jánosik, Artúr Nádor, Nagy Zoltán Lóránt, and László Bence Simon study grid patterns in this 2026 math paper. They ask for the maximum size of a subset of the n by n integer grid that avoids specific geometric configurations. The problem is a variation on classical work begun by Erdős and Purdy. Extremal problems ask how large a set can be before a pattern must appear.

Three-point patterns, such as collinear triples and right triangles, are well studied. Four-point configurations in the grid are much less explored. The team works on avoiding configurations of small size. Readers get new bounds and constructions in a corner of discrete geometry with many open cases.
arxiv-2601-14565:
Dylan Danese and four co-authors work on quantum measurements of time in this 2026 paper. The temporal degree of freedom of light is powerful for modern quantum technologies. It enables large-scale quantum computing architectures and record key-rates in quantum key distribution. Yet one task stays a unique experimental challenge.

That task is the generalized measurement of large, complex quantum superpositions of a photon's time of arrival. The team works on programming such measurements inside a complex medium. A complex medium scrambles light in rich ways, which can be turned into a tool. Readers get methods for measuring when a photon arrives, even when its time state is a broad superposition.
arxiv-2601-15465:
Mehrnoosh Sadat Shirvani and eight co-authors look at chatbots that copy the user in a 2026 arXiv paper. As digital tools take a larger role in mental health care, these self-clone bots offer a new kind of support. A self-clone is trained on a person's own chat patterns. Users can then talk with a digital copy of themselves. The authors frame this as a path to self-exploration and self-derived support.

The promise comes with clear risks, and the paper takes them head-on. A clone may blur a user's sense of identity. It may reinforce harmful thoughts rather than ease them. It may also blur who is in control of the exchange. The authors build a framework for design that keeps such bots safe and therapeutic.
arxiv-2601-15565:
Alex Terrasson and three co-authors build a bright source of squeezed light in a 2026 arXiv paper. Squeezed states of light cut noise below the standard quantum limit. That allows more precise measurement than classical light permits. One target use is nonlinear microscopy. There, performance is limited by two things: photodamage to the sample and quantum-limited noise. Brighter squeezed light could ease both limits.

The title calls the source pulsed and bright. Pulses suit microscopy, where samples can only take so much light. Quantum-enhanced precision is the goal named in the title. If the source works as hoped, microscopes could image delicate samples more gently. They could also pick out finer detail at the same light dose. The work sits where quantum optics meets practical imaging.
arxiv-2601-15665:
Kwang-il Seon and a large team set out a science theme for the K-DRIFT project in a 2026 arXiv paper. The theme joins two faint targets in the sky. One is galactic cirrus: wispy dust clouds in our own galaxy. The other is the circumgalactic medium, the gas halo around galaxies. The record's abstract opens with the note that galaxies are surrounded by such material, then turns to author and institute lines. Korean astronomy institutes lead the author list.

Faint, diffuse light is hard to image, yet it traces how galaxies gain and lose gas. A survey theme paper like this tells the community what the project will chase and why it matters.
arxiv-2601-15965:
Yongda Zhu and a large team study clumps inside young galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Massive star-forming clumps are a prominent feature of high-redshift galaxies. They may trace gravitational fragmentation in gas-rich disks. They may also trace feedback and the growth of galactic bulges. The team analyzes clump-like structures statistically. Their sample holds about 3,600 galaxies. Redshifts run from about two to eight, deep in cosmic time.

The images come from deep JWST NIRCam data in the JADES GOODS-South field. Mass scaling and radial trends are the paper's focus, per the title. How clump mass varies, and where clumps sit in their galaxies, test formation theories. Big samples turn anecdotes about clumps into population facts that models must match.
arxiv-2601-15265:
Wiesław Płaczek, Maciej Skrzypek, Bennie F. L. Ward, and Scott A. Yost review two workhorse simulation tools for electron-positron colliders. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Bhabha scattering, the collision of an electron with a positron. Two Monte Carlo generators cover the process.

BHLUMI handles small-angle scattering, and BHWIDE handles large angles. Both must be extremely precise, since Bhabha events calibrate a collider's luminosity. The authors present the tools in brief and discuss how to improve them. The planned future electron-positron colliders set the high precision bar they must meet in practice.
arxiv-2601-16065:
Chenyang Li and a large team trim waste tokens in robot vision and action models. Their 2026 preprint notes a flaw in such models. By default, the models may gaze too much at parts of the view that do not serve the task. The team calls those parts stray tokens. Stray gaze can hurt the acts the robot picks.

Their fix, named DTP, cuts stray tokens from the chain. The cut keeps gaze on the parts that guide the act. A lean chain should run fast and act with more care. The method is framed as plain yet strong. It targets models that join sight, words and acts for robot tasks in real rooms.
arxiv-2601-16165:
Mikhail Ivanov and coauthors rerun the first DESI data set for tight cosmos values. Their 2026 preprint joins many DESI probes in one fit. DESI maps star systems to trace how space grows. The fit uses the field theory of large scale form. It adds photo based star sets and lens cross links as well.

The team also pushes the three point fit to smaller scales. All parts use one firm frame for the fit. Tight joint fits test if the cosmos frame holds as one. They also weigh the case for the plain mass rank of neutrinos. The work gives per cent grade bounds from the joint data.
arxiv-2601-16665:
J. Seo writes on quantum machine learning, where computers use quantum states to learn from data. Quantum neural nets can hold rich patterns with ease. Yet training them on near-term machines is hard. Their error curves swing up and down a lot. Noise in the hardware adds to the strain. Seo's 2026 paper seeks a steadier way to train.

Most training now tweaks weights by small steps down a slope. That path can be slow and jumpy. It can also stick at sharp, poor spots. Seo puts forth a fix based on algebra. The fix uses weights tied to chance, to smooth the search. The goal is faster, calmer learning on real quantum gear.
arxiv-2601-16865:
Rowan Cherodian and Guy Tchuente build a new tool for cause work with weak mean shifts. Some policy shifts move a trait's whole spread, not its mean. A shift may lift the low tail while the mean stays put. Old cause tools key on mean moves and miss this case. Their 2026 preprint names this trait distributional relevance.

Their tool reads cause from the full spread shift. A quantile least squares fit does the gauge work. Such shifts show up in wage, school, and health plans. A tool that sees them can judge plans more fair. It keeps real gains from view loss by blunt means.
arxiv-2601-17465:
Akram Youssry and five co-authors boost quantum sensors with graybox machine learning. Quantum sensors beat classical ones in sharpness and sensitivity. In practice, noise and flawed control drag them down. State preparation is never perfect either. A graybox model mixes known physics with learned parts. It can absorb those unmodelled effects.

That mix aims to keep quantum gains in real labs. Uses span materials science and healthcare. Sensors that hold up outside ideal tests widen that reach. The work gives sensor teams a way to learn the flaws they cannot write down. It treats the device as it is, not as theory wishes it were.
arxiv-2601-17665:
Shan Gao comments on a claim about the Aharonov-Bohm phase. That phase shifts a charged particle even in field-free zones. Marletto and Vedral argued it is locally mediated. Their model uses entanglement between the particle and the quantized field. They claimed gauge independence for non-closed paths. Gao critically analyzes that model.

He argues the phase arises from interaction in a way their account misses. The debate is about what counts as local in quantum physics. Locality claims shape how field theory is taught and used. A sharp comment keeps a bold claim honest. Gao's record includes two papers on this effect in this set. The comment serves readers who track the locality debate.
arxiv-2601-17765:
Julius Giesler writes on a deep topic in algebraic geometry called Jacobian rings. His 2026 preprint links those rings to a part of Hodge theory for a smooth surface inside a torus. The link runs through a quotient space built from a lattice. The paper sets up a period map, which tracks how the shape of a variety shifts as its terms change.

Giesler then studies the slope of that map and works out its kernel in clear terms. The kernel is pinned down with the help of Laurent polynomials. As a payoff, the work bears on the infinitesimal Torelli theorem. That theorem asks when the period data is rich enough to fix the variety itself. Precise results here serve pure geometry.
arxiv-2601-17865:
Jia Gu, Liang Pang, Huawei Shen, and Xueqi Cheng study a trade-off at the heart of language models. Their 2026 preprint names two model types, D-models and E-models. The same next-token scores that drive a model also guide search, buying choices, and agent actions. So how a model samples its next step has effects far past the chat window. Spread and steadiness pull against each other.

A model that samples widely gives varied outputs but can drift off track. A model that plays safe can turn dull or stuck. The paper frames this as a diversity-stability trade-off. It studies how sampling choices shape that balance. The stakes grow as models take on more tasks where each next step is a real choice with real costs.
arxiv-2601-18065:
Aryan Roy, Zekun Wang, and Christopher J. MacLellan ask whether seeing makes a model more human in how it feels word concreteness. Their 2026 preprint compares vision-language models with text-only ones. People sense that some words name things you can touch, while others name abstract ideas. The team tests whether models share that sensitivity. They run a controlled comparison between matched Llama text backbones and their vision counterparts, using text-only prompts for both.

Keeping the prompts text-only makes the test fair. Any edge for the vision models must come from what image training taught them. The result bears on how grounding shapes language skill. It also informs debates about whether text alone can teach human-like word sense.
arxiv-2601-16365:
Yu Wei Soh and co-authors map the magnetic structure of a thin film of the compound EuZn2Sb2. The film is grown as a single crystal. It belongs to a class of materials where magnetism and charge transport are tightly linked. In such materials, the europium spins and the charge carriers sway each other in strong ways. That link is what the team sets out to map.

The 2026 preprint studies how the spins order inside the film. Work of this kind matters because the magnetic order steers the electrical behavior. A clear map of the structure gives later work a firm base. It shows where the spins point and how they line up across the film.
arxiv-2601-18965:
Sabrina Poulsen and a large team hunt for planets around dead stars with the James Webb telescope. Their survey, called MEAD, images nearby white dwarfs, the dense cores left when stars like the Sun die. It points Webb's mid-infrared camera at dozens of these stars, all close to Earth.

The team looks for extra infrared glow, dips from gas effects, and faint companions near each dwarf. Around one star, WD 0644+025, the excess glow points to a probable planet. A planet that outlives its star's death would tell us how planetary systems end and what can survive.
arxiv-2601-19165:
Yi Lyu, Yiyin Shen, and Takashi Matsuzawa build the simplest database system that can still teach the craft. A database management system stores and processes large data sets and can optimize freely, as long as results stay correct and ordered. The authors draw on a known undergraduate course at UW-Madison.

Their prototype strips the system to its bare teaching core. Students can read the whole thing and see how storage, queries, and correctness fit together. A small, clear system serves learning better than a vast pro tool whose internals no beginner can hold in mind at once.
arxiv-2601-19665:
Yan Jiang and six colleagues work on keeping power grids stable after a disturbance. When a fault hits, the grid's frequency swings and must be brought back. Modern inverter-based devices can shape the average frequency of the whole system nicely. In weakly connected grids, though, that average hides swings between areas.

Those inter-area oscillations can damage equipment or trigger wider failures. The authors develop a frequency shaping control aimed at damping them. Their design uses a root locus method, a classic tool for tuning feedback systems. The control is meant for grids where regions are tied by weak lines. As renewable inverters replace spinning machines, such controls become central to grid safety.
arxiv-2601-19865:
C. Munting and five colleagues report lab tests of using lasers to control electron beams. Future colliders like the FCC-ee need bunches of matched intensity. An instability called flip-flop can grow when colliding bunches differ in strength. Laser-driven Compton backscattering has been proposed to trim bunch intensity.

Lasers have also been proposed as indestructible collimators, scraping off stray beam particles without material jaws. The team tests these laser control ideas in the laboratory. Proof at small scale comes before any collider adopts the schemes. Beam control is a quiet bottleneck in collider design. The results inform whether light can do a job now done by matter.
arxiv-2601-19965:
Mingxuan Luo and colleagues tackle a misleading metric in online recommendation. Conversion rate counts clicks that end in purchase. It ignores refunds, so it overstates how happy users really are. Net conversion rate instead counts purchases that are kept, better reflecting true satisfaction and business value.

Predicting it is hard because of cascaded delay feedback: refunds arrive long after clicks and purchases. The authors present a benchmark, insights, and solutions for this prediction problem. Industrial recommender systems allocate traffic by such predictions, so errors waste money and annoy users. A metric that counts kept purchases aligns ranking with real outcomes. The work brings the delay structure of refunds into the model design.
arxiv-2601-20065:
Rishabh Sharma, Chitrasen Jena, and Volodymyr Vovchenko study the cooling phase of heavy-ion collisions. After quarks and gluons recombine, the system lives briefly as a gas of hadrons. That hadronic phase shapes the final abundances of particles detectors count. The authors model gold-gold collisions at RHIC across a wide energy range.

Their model is a hadron resonance gas in partial chemical equilibrium. It tracks how abundances freeze as the system cools and expands. Matching the model to data across energies tests our picture of the collision's late stage. The hadronic phase is easy to overlook next to the quark-gluon plasma. Yet it edits the very yields used to claim plasma properties. Careful modelling keeps those claims honest.
arxiv-2601-20265:
Yuenong Ling and Adrian Lozano-Duran build a subgrid-scale stress model for large-eddy simulation of turbulent flows. Such simulations resolve big eddies and model the small ones. Their model extends a data-assimilation approach so that the learned stress agrees with the numerical scheme of the flow solver itself.

The method handles flows with two directions of variation and is applied to turbulent boundary layers under adverse pressure gradients. Those are the flows along wings and blades where prediction is hardest. A model that matches the solver's own math could give steadier, more accurate results for engineering design.
arxiv-2601-20465:
Yang Li and four colleagues present BMAM, a brain-inspired memory framework for language model agents. Agents that act over long horizons struggle to keep time-grounded information and stay consistent across sessions. The authors name this failure soul erosion. BMAM models memory as a set of specialized subsystems rather than one unstructured store.

Each subsystem plays a distinct role, echoing how brains divide memory work. The architecture is meant to be general-purpose, serving agents of many kinds. Agents that remember who said what, and when, could serve users over months without slowly drifting away from their instructions and facts.
arxiv-2601-18365:
Giovanni Barbarino writes a short note on a topic in graph theory, the study of networks made of points and links. For a plain graph, one can build a blended table that mixes two simpler tables. One table shows which points are linked. The other lists how many links each point has. A single dial sets how much of each table goes into the blend.

Barbarino looks at the largest value that comes out of that blended table. Two past claims gave floors for that value, and it was not clear which floor was higher. He shows that one floor beats the other, as long as no point in the graph sits alone with no links at all. Notes like this keep the tools of the field sharp for later work on networks.
arxiv-2601-18465:
Mihir Durve and five colleagues study how drops of water move on live leaves, and they find that the leaf charges it-self as drops slide. How a drop runs, sticks, or slips on a leaf shapes how the plant deals with rain and dew. Those same moves guide the design of new stuff that sheds or holds water by plan.

The team show that a charge builds on the leaf skin as drops pass. That charge then pulls back on the next drops and shifts how they run. A force that teams had not weighed thus turns out to shape the whole dance. The find could change how plant staff read leaf wetness. It could also spark new films and coats that use charge to steer drops.
arxiv-2601-18865:
Rei Nishiura, Shoma Kamijima, and Kunihito Ioka study how a fierce radio burst can be bent by the cloud it is born in. The bursts are brief, bright flashes from far space. Some come from stars with huge fields, called magnetars. In-side that field sits a thin soup of bits and their anti-twins. A burst that climbs out must pass that soup, and the soup can scatter it.

The team check old maths of that scatter with a sim that tracks each bit. They find the scatter, though curbed by the field, still grows step by step till it must shape the burst. That growth could dim some bursts or stretch them in time. It sets a trait that burst tools should look for. A match in real bursts would back the maths and map the soup at the burst's birth.
arxiv-2601-21365:
Prateek Puri warns that small AI models pose safety risks that current policy largely ignores. AI brings clear gains to fields like medicine and materials work. Most governance so far, though, judges risk by the computing power behind a model.

Small models need little compute, so they slip under those thresholds. Yet they can still be capable, cheap to copy, and easy to misuse. The paper maps the challenges these models create for oversight. It argues that rules based on size alone will miss a growing class of threats. Policy, the author urges, should track what models can do, not just their cost.
arxiv-2601-21665:
Vijini Liyanage and François Yvon adapt word-piece tokenizers to special domains. Tokenization chops text into pieces that a language model reads. Standard practice trains one general tokenizer for everything, then uses it for training and serving alike.

A generic piece set wastes effort on text from narrow fields or specific languages. Rare terms get shredded into many tiny pieces, which costs speed and accuracy. The authors adapt the popular BPE method to build specialized tokenizers. A fitted tokenizer could make domain models, from law to medicine, cheaper to run and sharper on their own vocabulary.
arxiv-2601-22365:
Yisi Ke and five co-authors use large language models to attack a famed open guess about tree lengths. The Gilbert-Pollak guess says a Steiner tree, which may add new points, can beat a plain spanning tree by only a set margin. Their 2026 preprint takes the plane case, open since 1968.

The team set models to hunt for proofs, counter-cases, or new bounds. A machine-led search can scan far more shapes than a human team. Win or lose, the hunt shows what models can do in hard math. It may also crack a guess that has stood for decades.
arxiv-2601-22765:
Rohit Varma and Santosh Nannuru complete distance matrices the Bayesian way, under geometric rules. A Euclidean distance matrix holds all pair gaps between points; often only a few, noisy gaps are known. Their 2026 preprint notes that the task feeds sensor location, room acoustics, and molecule shape work.

Older tools use rank tricks or semidefinite programs to enforce the geometry. A Bayesian route adds honest doubt ranges to each filled gap. That doubt matters when the map guides real choices. The work blends geometry with sound inference. It aims for maps that know their limits.
arxiv-2601-21765:
Augusto Fasano and Giovanni Rebaudo, based in Torino, work on a common statistical problem. Picking which variables matter when the outcome is simply yes or no. Their approach is Bayesian. It uses a probit link for the binary outcome. Its prior lets most coefficients sit at zero while a few stand out.

The standard tool for such models, Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, gets painfully slow when the data have many dimensions. The 2026 preprint instead develops a mean-field variational Bayes method, which replaces slow sampling with a faster approximation. Fast, reliable variable selection matters wherever binary outcomes are predicted from many possible factors, from medicine to economics and social science.
arxiv-2601-21965:
Deeksha Shama, Dimitra Emmanouilidou, and Ivan Tashev work on measuring mental effort from brain signals in real time. Brain-computer interfaces that adapt to how engaged a user is need a reliable read on cognitive load. Brain waves recorded by EEG offer a cheap, non-invasive way to get that signal.

Older methods, though, struggle when a new person wears the headset, and they often need training for one specific task. The team's 2026 preprint uses brain foundation models, large models pretrained on neural data, together with interpretability tools. Their aim is load estimation that transfers across people and tasks, which would make adaptive learning systems and assistive interfaces far more practical.
arxiv-2601-22065:
Ksenija Kovalenka and co-authors show that mess can create a phase of matter, not just kill one. In clean solids, some phases guard the flow of charge in odd ways. Dirt and flaws tend to blur those phases. The team uses a toy model of such a phase, the Haldane model, to ask what dirt does in truth.

They find that dirt does more than shift the edge of a phase. It can hold open a new phase that clean solids do not show. In that phase, the guard on charge flow exists thanks to the dirt itself. Their work is a hint to labs: a bit of mess, placed with care, may give solids traits that pure ones lack.
arxiv-2601-20865:
Emmanuel Pio Pastore and Francesco De Rango argue that some immune complexity cannot be computed at all. Their 2026 paper gives a certificate-based view of immune reactions. The frame rests on algorithmic information theory. A fixed executor maps a short advice string to a candidate response. A response counts only if a validity check accepts it. That check may be decidable or only semi-decidable.

Gaps then appear between what can be certified and what can be computed. The authors call these information gaps under effective constraints. The immune system is their test case for deep limits on prediction. If this complexity is noncomputable, no algorithm can shortcut the biology. The paper joins immunology with the math of what can be known.
arxiv-2601-20965:
Drake Deming and eight co-authors propose a third way to probe the air of rocky planets. Their 2026 paper concerns temperate exoplanets, worlds that could hold liquid water. Detecting their atmospheres has proven hard for JWST. Transit spectroscopy of the TRAPPIST-1 planets suffers from spots and faculae on the host star. Secondary eclipses have found hot rocks, but evidence for atmospheres stays elusive. A new observable is needed.

The authors champion color phase curves. A phase curve tracks a planet's light as it orbits. Color adds which wavelengths rise and fall. Together they can betray an atmosphere without a transit. The paper lays out this option for temperate rocky worlds. It offers observers a path around stellar contamination. The idea could guide future telescope time toward clearer answers.
arxiv-2601-21165:
Miles Wang and a large team of co-authors, including OpenAI staff, build a test of expert-level science skill for AI. Their 2026 paper introduces FrontierScience. The benchmark evaluates AI capabilities for expert-level scientific reasoning. It consists of two tracks. The Olympiad track holds international olympiad problems at the level of the physics, chemistry, and biology olympiads. The Research track holds PhD-level, open-ended problems. Those mirror sub-problems in real scientific research.

Most benchmarks top out at undergraduate knowledge. FrontierScience aims at the frontier its name claims. Open-ended research problems resist simple grading, so the design matters. The benchmark can track whether AI systems approach working-scientist ability. It also exposes where they still fail like students. Labs and funders get a sterner yardstick for scientific AI.
arxiv-2512-01365:
Swati Kumari and co-authors build a guard for networks in smart devices. Homes and plants now link many small devices to the web. Odd traffic on those links can signal an attack. Spotting that traffic fast is a key safety task.

Their method mixes quantum and classic computing. A quantum support vector tool sorts traffic as normal or odd. A quantum wavelet step cleans the signal first. The mix is tested under the noise of today's small quantum machines. Strong scores would hint that quantum aids can help guard real device networks.
arxiv-2512-01465:
Hongnan Si and co-authors fill gaps in water quality data. Sensors that track river and lake health can fail. Long records then hold holes where data is lost. Holes make trend checks and alerts hard to trust.

Their network blends convolution with a Tucker form. That form squeezes the data while keeping its main traits. The net learns from the sound parts to rebuild the lost parts. Full records help staff spot pollution early. They also give a truer view of how water health shifts over months and years. The squeeze form also keeps time order intact, so seasonal swings and slow drifts in water health stay visible after gaps are filled.
arxiv-2512-01565:
Alex Oshin and co-authors speed up nonlinear programming with deep unfolding. Quadratic programs sit inside many control and planning tasks. Solvers must stay feasible at each step, which can be slow. Their solver, FlexQP, is built to stay feasible by design.

Deep unfolding turns solver steps into a learnable network. Training tunes those steps for speed on real task families. An always-feasible solver can run in tight loops, like robot control. Learned speed with firm feasibility could cut compute in autonomous systems. Unfolded steps keep solver structure, so the learned solver stays readable to control engineers who must certify it before real use.
arxiv-2512-01865:
Adel Moumen, Guangzhi Sun, and Philip Woodland interleave languages to lift speech language models. Speech models learn language straight from audio units. That widens access for tongues with little written text. Progress has stayed English-centric due to scarce data and tests elsewhere.

Cross-lingual interleaving mixes speech units across languages in training. Shared structure can then transfer to low-resource tongues. The team tests whether that transfer holds in practice. Gains would bring voice tools to many communities now left out of language technology. Interleaving needs no parallel corpora, a key gain for tongues where aligned speech pairs across languages simply do not exist yet.
arxiv-2512-01065:
Carlos Martínez-Ranero and Lucas Polymeris construct a set-theoretic model with a rare combination in a 2025 paper. Suslin lines are dense linear orders with special countability properties, long studied in set theory. The Open Graph Axiom is a statement about coloring edges of large graphs, with strong consequences for such orders.

The authors build a model where the Open Graph Axiom holds, yet a 2-entangled Suslin line exists. As a consequence, that model has a 2-entangled uncountable linear order, but no such order that is separable. Careful models like this show which combinations of axioms can coexist.
arxiv-2601-22665:
Mayukh Mukherjee and Utsab Sarkar study sharp thresholds in boundary problems on curved spaces. The problems involve the Escobar quotient and a family of Gagliardo–Nirenberg functionals, both tied to how shapes bend and stretch. On compact manifolds with boundary, solutions can either settle or blow up in bubbles.

Their unified framework sorts when each outcome happens, using chart-scale maps and stability checks. They also reduce hard cases to finite-dimensional ones under set conditions. Such results guide the study of optimal shapes and inequalities in geometry. The framework covers both attainment and bubbling cases, the two fates that compete in these boundary-critical variational problems.
arxiv-2601-23065:
Xijie Yang and six co-authors rebuild indoor scenes so they can be edited with correct lighting. Radiance-field methods like NeRF copy rooms with high visual fidelity, but edits fail because lighting is baked in. Physically based rendering handles light properly, yet needs exact geometry that real rooms rarely provide.

Their EAG-PT joins emission-aware Gaussians with path tracing to get both fidelity and editability. Rooms that relight correctly can be restyled for design, film, and virtual tours. The blend aims to end the choice between pretty and editable.
arxiv-2601-23265:
Dawei Zhu and five co-authors present PaperBanana, an agent framework that draws academic illustrations automatically. AI scientists powered by language models now run much of the research workflow. Producing publication-ready figures, though, remains a labor-intensive bottleneck done by hand.

PaperBanana aims to lift that burden with an agentic pipeline for diagrams and illustrations. Automatic figures matched to a paper's content could speed every stage of writing and review. The work targets the unglamorous steps that quietly consume researcher time. Publication-ready output is the bar, not rough sketches, because journals demand figures that survive print production.
arxiv-2512-00365:
People reason about physical objects through rough internal body representations, coarse shapes that capture an object's extent. Andrey Gizdov and co-authors test whether vision models develop comparable representations in 2025. Human psychophysics suggests we use such approximations for intuitive predictions about motion and physics.

The team probes models trained for segmentation, asking whether their internal structure contains body-like representations. The internal structure of human representations remains largely unknown, so models offer a testable comparison. Findings could connect machine perception to cognitive science and improve models that must predict how objects will move and collide. Segmentation models are a good probe because they must carve the world into objects.
arxiv-2512-00265:
Estimating cause and effect with instrumental variables gets hard when there are more parameters than observations. Eleftheria Kelekidou writes an exposition in 2025 on high-dimensional penalized linear instrumental variable estimation. The methods covered are BRIDGE and adaptive LASSO, used inside two-stage least squares.

Both stages of the procedure can have parameter counts that grow with the sample size. Penalization keeps such problems solvable by shrinking weak coefficients toward zero. The exposition helps applied researchers in economics and health choose and understand tools for settings where traditional instrumental variable methods break down. Two-stage least squares is the classic estimator the penalized methods extend. Growing parameter counts are now routine in genetic and economic instruments. For folks who work with scant data and many loose ends, the gain is a set of tools that stay put. They hold up when the old rules break down at scale.
arxiv-2512-03265:
Heat that spreads and fades follows patterns over long times. Carmen Cortázar, Fernando Quirós, and Noemí Wolanski study a nonlocal heat equation in this 2025 work. Nonlocal means heat jumps across distance, not just to nearby points, and an absorption term removes heat.

The authors focus on the case where absorption dominates and the starting heat decays fast. They describe how solutions behave after long times. Such results help model spread in biology and materials where long jumps occur. They also test the limits of classic diffusion theory. Long-time limits reveal the final shape of a solution, long after early details fade.
arxiv-2512-02165:
The Higgs boson occasionally decays into pairs of photons, or a photon and a Z boson, and these rare decays are precision tests of particle physics. Alexander Khodjamirian, Kirill Melnikov, and Arkady Vainshtein estimate in 2025 the leading corrections to those decays that come from non-perturbative effects in the strong force.

The corrections originate in how light quarks contribute to the decay, a corner where perturbative calculation, the usual step-by-step method, runs out. Sizing them up tells experimenters how much of any future mismatch with theory could be mundane strong-force physics. Rare Higgs decays are prized because new particles could shift them, so every known contribution must be accounted for first.
arxiv-2512-02265:
Clinical machine learning must be accurate, fair across patient groups, and explainable enough for doctors to trust, and improving one can disturb the others. Joshua Anderson and Shyam Visweswaran examine in 2025 a neglected link in that triangle: how enforcing fairness changes a model's explanations.

It was already known that fairness work can move predictive performance, but its effect on explainability was little studied. If explanations shift when fairness is enforced, clinicians may see different reasons for the same prediction, which affects trust. The study maps that interaction for healthcare models, where explanations are an essential ingredient of safe use.
arxiv-2512-02465:
Xingwang Li and nine co-authors tackle a practical gap in city weather data: rain gauges are sparse. Fast city growth and more extreme storms make fine grained rain maps vital for safer, smarter cities. Their 2025 study uses signals from commercial microwave links, the radio links that carry phone traffic.

Those links weaken when rain crosses them, so they can act as rough rain sensors. The team presents TabGRU, a design that reads link data to estimate how hard rain falls across a city. Such low cost sensing could help cities track storms street by street. City crews could use such maps to warn streets that face fast floods.
arxiv-2512-02665:
Jing Ma tests whether the order of documents changes what a language model concludes from them. Models now summarize several long documents at once, as in AI search overviews. Whether they weigh every source equally has been unclear.

Ma built forty triplets of news articles on abortion, mixing pro, neutral, and opposing views. Each triplet was fed in all six possible orders to Gemini 2.5 Flash, which wrote a neutral overview. Comparing outputs across orders shows if early or late placement tilts the summary, a fairness concern for news synthesis. That tilt, if real, means the same facts can read as slanted or fair based on list order alone.
plos-pone-0010065:
Janet Higgins, Paul Bailey, and David Laurie compared flowering genes across grasses in 2010. Their PLOS ONE study used Brachypodium distachyon as the model plant. That small grass stands in for temperate cereals such as barley, wheat, and oats. Flowering time decides when those crops set seed, so its control genes matter to farming.

The authors compared Brachypodium genes with those of rice and the model plant Arabidopsis. Shared and divergent pathways show which flowering controls are old and which are grass-specific. Such maps help breeders tune flowering to local seasons and a changing climate.
plos-pone-0010165:
Steve Bellan reconsidered a basic assumption in disease models in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most models of mosquito-borne disease assume mosquitoes die at a constant rate. New field research, though, suggests death rates often depend on mosquito age. That difference can change how diseases like malaria spread and how control measures perform.

Bellan built a simple model that lets mosquito mortality vary with age. He also weighed the extrinsic incubation period, the time a parasite needs inside the mosquito. More realistic survival curves can shift which control strategies look best on paper.
plos-pone-0010265:
The authors were Ana Ferreira, Rodrigo Ferreira, Dimple Rajgor, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study watched doctors reason through real cases. Little was known about how physicians actually make decisions in practice. Diagnostic guidelines assume a tidier logic than real clinics allow, so the team recorded reasoning in a real life environment.

From transcripts of that reasoning, they argue real clinical thinking runs on bounded rationality. Doctors use good-enough shortcuts under time and information limits. Guidelines that ignore those limits, they suggest, will keep missing how diagnosis really happens at the bedside.
plos-pone-0010365:
Abhik Bandyopadhyay and colleagues combined two cancer drugs in mouse breast tumors for PLOS ONE in 2010. A change in tumor cells, called EMT, can make cancers spread and resist drugs. A signal protein named TGF-beta strongly drives that change. The team paired a standard drug, doxorubicin, with a small compound that blocks TGF-beta. They tested the pair in mouse models of metastatic breast cancer.

Blocking the signal aimed to stop tumor cells from gaining stem-like traits. Those traits are tied to relapse after treatment. The drug pair thus attacks both the tumor bulk and its hardest cells. Mouse success is only a first step toward human use. Still, the logic of pairing a killer drug with an anti-spread drug is clearly laid out.
plos-pone-0009865:
Many biological models pulse in cycles, from heartbeats to daily rhythms. Mochamad Apri and colleagues offered a faster way to judge how robust such models are. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A robustness region is the range of settings where a model still behaves well. Oscillatory behavior means the model swings back and forth in a steady pattern. Estimating that region efficiently saves heavy computing time. Biological models are math versions of living processes. Modelers can then trust their models across wider conditions. Oscillations drive much of biology, from sleep to cell cycles.
plos-pone-0009965:
Measuring a fast chemical change inside cells usually takes slow, fussy lab work. Hector Aguilar and colleagues sped that measurement up with a high-throughput assay. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosin is the motor protein that powers muscle movement.

The change is phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain, a switch for muscle contraction. In-cell Western assays read the signal inside intact cells, in bulk. The authors compared the new assays with classic Western immunoblots. Faster quantification helps labs screen many samples at once. High-throughput means testing many samples in parallel.
